articles.title: House GOP launches defense plan to shield Trump from looming Democrat investigations
articles.summary: House GOP leadership letter from Steve Scalise warns committee chairs to prepare defenses against expected Democrat-led probes of Trump allies.
articles.body:
FIRST ON FOX: House GOP leadership is giving Republican lawmakers a new playbook to go up against an expected barrage of Democrat-led investigations in the new Congress.

Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., wrote a letter to the current chairs of House committees on Thursday warning them to "maximize our remaining days in power to prepare for what is coming" with instructions on how to brace for those expected probes. A source sent a copy of that letter to Fox News Digital.

"House Democrats have signaled they intend to impeach President Trump , but they will not stop there. They will weaponize every single gavel to appease their radical base," Scalise said. "They will use their oversight authorities to harass the President, his family, cabinet officials, and they will seek to destroy our allies. You all will be a key line of defense in this fight."

The guidance includes three key points: "taking inventory" of current and likely future investigative efforts by Democrats while they are in the minority, identifying who is on Democrats' target list, and reviewing how recent Supreme Court rulings as well as a Department of Justice (DOJ) memo on executive privilege could factor into future investigations.

Democrats' targets could include "administration officials, programs and authorities, and external allies, including conservative partners and industry leaders," Scalise said.

He added that his staff would meet with the relevant committees and others to further prepare.

"Please let me know if there are any additional tools or support you need from me as you undertake this important effort," Scalise wrote. "I have full confidence that we will be effective in our efforts to fight back as a team."

Democrats have signaled they are poised for a wide range of investigations targeting Trump's Cabinet, family, businesses, and allies as soon as they take over Congress next year.

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., the likely next head of the House Oversight Committee , released a brief statement Tuesday night when it was projected Democrats would win the House: "Lawyer up."

The committee said in the statement, "Following this win, Garcia will become Chairman of the House Oversight Committee, where he has vowed to take on the Trump Crime Family, corporate corruption, DHS and ICE abuses, and the cover-up of the Epstein files. His statement can be found below."

House Homeland Security Committee Democrats have similarly signaled they are preparing to probe Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin .

Meanwhile, a spokeswoman for House Judiciary Committee Democrats told Fox News Digital in response to Scalise's letter, "Sounds like Rep. Scalise is asking his fellow Republicans to compile a list of all the corruption, lawlessness, and abuse they've been protecting from congressional oversight. But the people have spoken, and the cover-up expires with the Republican majority. The days of invertebrate congressional submission are over."

The letter comes a day after Scalise launched a bid to become House minority leader in the new Congress.

He will be up against House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan , R-Ohio, for the job.

Fox News Digital reached out to Democrats on the House Oversight Committee for comment.

articles.standfirst: Campanha antirrábica acontece neste sábado (7), das 8h às 17h, e atende animais a partir dos três meses de idade, incluindo aqueles que precisam receber a segunda dose.
articles.summary: Campanha ocorre das 8h às 17h e atende cães e gatos a partir dos três meses. A ação também busca revacinar animais que receberam a primeira dose.

A Prefeitura de Juiz de Fora vai disponibilizar 38 pontos de vacinação contra a raiva para cães e gatos neste sábado (7), das 8h às 17h. Confira a lista mais abaixo .

A campanha busca revacinar animais que receberam a primeira dose em setembro, na etapa inicial, e atender tutores que ainda não conseguiram imunizar seus pets.

A vacina é indicada para cães e gatos a partir dos três meses de idade e não apresenta contraindicações gerais. No caso de fêmeas gestantes ou que estejam amamentando, é necessário ter cuidado durante a aplicação para evitar situações de estresse.

Animais que apresentarem comportamento muito agitado nesses períodos devem ser avaliados, já que a vacinação pode não ser recomendada naquele momento.

Para receber a dose, os animais devem ser levados por um adulto. Os cães precisam estar com guia e coleira, enquanto os de grande porte ou com comportamento agressivo devem usar focinheira. Já os gatos devem ser transportados em caixas apropriadas.

articles.title: Papa envia mensagem a Lula ao passar por espaço aéreo brasileiro  | G1
articles.standfirst: Pontífice está em viagem pela América do Sul, que contará com agendas no Uruguai, Argentina e Peru.
articles.summary: Pontífice está em viagem pela América do Sul, que contará com agendas no Uruguai, Argentina e Peru.
articles.body:
Papa Leão XIV acena antes de embarcar em avião para iniciar sua viagem à América Latina em 6 de novembro de 2026. — Foto: REUTERS/Remo Casilli

O papa Leão XIV, em viagem pela América do Sul, enviou uma mensagem ao presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT). Outros cinco chefes de estado receberam telegramas do pontífice.

“Ao sobrevoar o espaço aéreo brasileiro em minha Viagem Apostólica ao Uruguai, à Argentina e ao Peru, envio cordiais saudações a Vossa Excelência e aos seus cidadãos, e invoco sobre a nação os dons da unidade e da paz de Deus Todo-Poderoso.”

A passagem do papa Leão XIV pelo continente contará com agendas no Uruguai, na Argentina e no Peru. O primeiro compromisso oficial foi na manhã desta sexta-feira (6) em Montevidéu, capital uruguaia.

Durante as mais de 13 horas de voo, o pontífice enviou saudações aos países sobrevoados. A começar pela própria Itália, quando decolou do Aeroporto Internacional Leonardo da Vinci, em Fiumicino, na grande Roma.

Em uma rede social, o presidente Lula agradeceu a mensagem e fez um convite ao papa Leão XIV para que visite o Brasil.

"Recebi com alegria a mensagem do Papa Leão XIV, que enviou bênçãos de unidade e paz ao povo brasileiro. Agradeço de coração o carinho de Sua Santidade e reitero o convite para que visite o Brasil. Será recebido de braços abertos, com muito afeto e fé'", disse o presidente brasileiro em resposta ao pontífice.

A declaração foi feita ainda a bordo do avião que o levava a Montevidéu.

A contagem dos votos da disputa legislativa ainda está acontecendo. Porém, os resultados parciais já monstram uma avanço expressivo do partido Democrata contra o Republicano, que abriga o presidente Donald Trump.

Leão entrou para a história como o primeiro pontífice a participar de uma eleição norte-americana.

O papa também disse que está se sentindo relativamente bem após passar por uma cirurgia para tratar um câncer no pulmão no mês passado .

Aos 71 anos, o pontífice disse que a experiência com o tratamento contra o câncer reforçou sua convicção de que o acesso à saúde é um direito humano.

articles.title: Lula diz que será 'fiscal' de entregas do governo: 'Quem não quiser fazer, cai fora' | G1
articles.standfirst: Cobrança ocorre agora em um novo contexto político. Lula foi reeleito em outubro e inicia o quarto mandato em janeiro de 2027.
articles.summary: Cobrança ocorre agora em um novo contexto político. Lula foi reeleito em outubro e inicia o quarto mandato em janeiro de 2027.
articles.body:
O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) afirmou nesta sexta-feira (6) que passará a fiscalizar o cumprimento e os prazos das medidas aprovadas pelo governo . Segundo Lula , quem não estiver disposto a executar as decisões terá de deixar a gestão.

“A partir de agora, além da Casa Civil, o Lulinha vai ser fiscal do cumprimento de cada coisa que a gente aprovar. Aprovou uma coisa, eu quero saber a data de entrega. E também quanto tempo. Quem não quiser fazer, cai fora. Porque o Brasil não pode esperar”, afirmou.

A declaração foi dada durante reunião extraordinária do Conselho Nacional de Política Energética (CNPE), em Brasília.

Em agosto de 2025, durante uma reunião ministerial para fazer um balanço da gestão e projetar as entregas até o fim do mandato, o presidente já havia reclamado que o governo “não tem mais muito tempo” e cobrado que ministros levassem problemas até ele.

A cobrança ocorre agora em um novo contexto político. Lula foi reeleito em outubro e inicia o quarto mandato em janeiro de 2027. O plano apresentado na eleição contém uma série de compromissos para áreas como renda, emprego, impostos, aposentadoria, crédito e moradia.

O próximo governo também deverá enfrentar um Congresso com maioria de oposição. O PT e partidos aliados terão menos espaço que siglas de oposição e centro, o que exigirá negociações para que Lula consiga transformar propostas em medidas efetivas.

Lula durante reunião do CNPE. — Foto: Tauan Alencar/MME

A fala desta sexta acrescenta um elemento à cobrança que Lula já vinha fazendo sobre a equipe: o presidente afirmou que pretende acompanhar pessoalmente datas e prazos de execução, além do monitoramento feito pela Casa Civil.

O acompanhamento das entregas também permite medir o que efetivamente saiu do papel. Em julho, levantamento do g1 avaliou o andamento das promessas assumidas por Lula na campanha de 2022 e classificou os compromissos entre cumpridos, cumpridos em parte e ainda não cumpridos. A análise considerou ações realizadas até junho de 2026.

A Casa Civil, comandada pela ministra Miriam Belchior, tem entre suas funções coordenar a execução de políticas públicas entre os ministérios. Ao dizer que será “fiscal”, Lula afirmou que também passará a acompanhar pessoalmente os prazos das medidas aprovadas.

O presidente defendeu a condução fiscal do governo e afirmou que eventuais medidas de ajuste não vão impor sacrifícios à população mais pobre. “A única coisa que eles têm que saber é que o pobre não pagará a conta”, declarou.

Lula fez a cobrança durante uma reunião do CNPE, principal órgão de assessoramento da Presidência para políticas na área de energia.

O conselho é presidido pelo Ministério de Minas e Energia e reúne representantes do governo, da sociedade civil e de instituições de ensino.

O colegiado já serviu em outras ocasiões para definir medidas de impacto amplo. Em agosto de 2024, por exemplo, aprovou a Política Nacional de Transição Energética.

Em junho de 2025, voltou a se reunir com Lula para discutir políticas relacionadas aos combustíveis e à ampliação da mistura de biocombustíveis.

articles.title: Lula sobre corte de gastos: 'pobre não pagará conta' de ajuste | G1
articles.standfirst: Em meio a cobranças do mercado e de economistas por contenção orçamentária, petista afirma que compromisso fiscal não vai recair sobre a população de baixa renda.
articles.summary: Lula defende a seriedade fiscal do Brasil e garante que o corte de gastos e o ajuste no orçamento não vão recair sobre a população de baixa renda do país.
articles.body:
O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ( PT ) rebateu nesta sexta-feira (6) cobranças de economistas e do mercado financeiro por cortes de gastos . Ele afirmou que o governo tem responsabilidade social e "seriedade fiscal" e que o povo pobre do país não "pagará a conta" de medidas de ajuste.

Lula deu as declarações ao participar de uma reunião do Conselho Nacional de Política Energética (CNPE), no Ministério de Minas e Energia .

"Quantos países do mundo têm a seriedade fiscal que temos? Qual a dívida dos Estados Unidos? Da França? Do Japão? Da Itália? Perto da nossa, é o dobro, em relação ao PIB? E, se a gente for analisar a nossa dívida de verdade, ela nem é tudo que aparece", afirmou o petista.

Na sequência, Lula cobrou do ministro da Fazenda, Dario Durigan, que apresentasse à imprensa os dados sobre a dívida pública brasileira, destacando como era a situação fiscal do país quando o PT retornou ao poder em 2023.

"Para alguém falar que a gente não tem [responsabilidade], precisa dizer como a gente pegou esse governo. Se não disser como encontramos esse governo, as pessoas não têm comparativo", declarou Lula.

"A única coisa que eles têm que saber é que o pobre não pagará a conta. A única coisa é que nós não levaremos o povo pobre a nenhum sacrifício[...]. Nós pegamos esse governo com déficit de 2,8% e nós estamos entregando orçamento com superávit. Não é o que o sistema financeiro quer, porque ele quer tudo. É o que a gente pode fazer", acrescentou o petista.

Lula tem sido cobrado por especialistas em economia e pelo mercado financeiro a conter despesas obrigatórias, como despesas com Previdência, assistência social, funcionalismo, entre outras .

Essa ausência de freio nas despesas alimenta a desconfiança do mercado financeiro quanto à sustentabilidade da dívida pública , o que gera efeitos práticos na economia, como alta do dólar, aumento das expectativas de inflação e manutenção da taxa básica de juros (Selic) em patamares elevados por mais tempo.

Sem um sinal claro de disciplina fiscal, o custo do crédito para empresas e famílias sobe, encarece o financiamento da própria dívida do governo e desestimula o crescimento econômico.

Por outro lado, o governo resiste a cortes lineares sob o argumento de que investimentos sociais, saúde e educação não devem ser tratados como despesas descartáveis.

Lula e sua equipe defendem que o ajuste fiscal não recaia apenas sobre a população mais vulnerável, cobrando que o debate inclua também a redução de renúncias fiscais concedidas a setores empresariais e a revisão dos altos volumes destinados a emendas parlamentares.

'Ano menos exitoso do que eu gostaria', afirma Lula

No mesmo pronunciamento, Lula afirmou que o ano de 2026 está terminando de uma forma menos "exitosa" do que a que ele esperava, mas emendou declarando que o governo fez o possível no período.

"Agora estamos terminando o ano menos exitoso que eu gostaria. Gostaria que a economia estivesse crescendo 10%, desemprego zero, salário mínimo de R$ 5 mil. Gostaria [de] tudo bem maior, mas a gente consegue o que é possível construir", afirmou.

Apesar das críticas sobre as contas públicas, o petista voltou a dizer que tem como princípio a ideia de gastar menos do que arrecada, mas que vai manter a responsabilidade social do governo.

"O que precisamos fazer neste país é continuar dizendo o seguinte: este país vai continuar com responsabilidade social porque eu tive uma professora analfabeta, chamada dona Lindu [mãe de Lula], que pegava o meu pagamento no final do mês e dizia: 'Você não pode gastar o que você não tem'. Isso, que eu aprendi na minha vida, eu trouxe para o governo", concluiu.

O presidente Lula durante reunião no Ministério de Minas e Energia nesta sexta-feira (6) — Foto: Tauan Alencar/MME

articles.title: PDT aprova federação com Solidariedade, PRD e Avante por recursos | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo o partido, união permitirá que as quatro siglas superem a cláusula de barreira; ampliação será submetida ao TSE.
articles.summary: A cúpula do PDT aprovou a entrada em uma federação com Solidariedade, PRD e Avante para superar a cláusula de barreira e garantir acesso ao fundo partidário.
articles.body:
O presidente nacional do PDT, Carlos Lupi, durante convenção nacional do partido em Brasília — Foto: Reprodução/YouTube PDT

A Executiva Nacional do PDT aprovou nesta sexta-feira (6), em reunião híbrida, o ingresso do partido na federação com Solidariedade, PRD e Avante.

Segundo o PDT, a união permitirá que as quatro siglas superem, em conjunto, a cláusula de barreira e tenham acesso ao Fundo Partidário e direito à propaganda gratuita no rádio e na televisão.

O comando do partido também se posicionou favoravelmente à inclusão do PSB na aliança.

Criadas por uma lei de 2021, as federações permitem que dois ou mais partidos se unam para disputar eleições e atuar no Legislativo como se fossem uma única legenda. Cada sigla mantém seu nome e sua organização, mas todas devem atuar juntas em todo o país por pelo menos quatro anos.

Com a decisão, as legendas envolvidas encaminharão ao Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) o pedido de ampliação da federação. O nome e o estatuto da associação também serão atualizados.

O presidente nacional do PDT, Carlos Lupi, afirmou que a federação preserva a história do trabalhismo, garante a independência administrativa dos partidos e fortalece a atuação das bancadas no Congresso Nacional.

“A federação potencializará os partidos, incluindo nossos deputados e senadores, na defesa da democracia e dos direitos do povo brasileiro. É o legado trabalhista cada vez presente na vida dos brasileiros”, disse.

Lupi afirmou ainda que as negociações para atrair o PSB continuarão.

"Prosseguiremos com as discussões para agregar o PSB. São partidos que comungam de valores semelhantes e podem caminhar juntos nos próximos anos."

Atualmente, há cinco federações registradas no Tribunal Superior Eleitoral: PT-PCdoB-PV, PSDB-Cidadania, PSOL-Rede, PRD-Solidariedade e União Brasil-PP. O PDT e o Avante pretendem entrar na federação que já reúne PRD e Solidariedade. Portanto, a união ampliará um grupo já existente.

O PDT, o Avante, o Missão e a federação Renovação Solidária, formada por PRD e Solidariedade, ficaram abaixo dos requisitos da cláusula de barreira nas eleições de 2026 , apesar de terem elegido representantes para a Câmara dos Deputados.

Também chamada de cláusula de desempenho , a regra condiciona o acesso ao Fundo Partidário e à propaganda partidária gratuita no rádio e na televisão. Ficar abaixo dela não impede a posse dos deputados eleitos nem provoca o fechamento dos partidos.

Para superar a cláusula nas eleições deste ano, partidos e federações precisavam cumprir uma de duas exigências:

Obter ao menos 2,5% dos votos válidos nacionais para a Câmara, com um mínimo de 1,5% em pelo menos nove unidades da Federação;

Eleger ao menos 13 deputados federais, distribuídos por pelo menos nove unidades da Federação.

A federação PSOL/Rede também apareceu abaixo dos requisitos na apuração inicial. Embora tivesse superado o percentual nacional de votos, havia alcançado o mínimo estadual em apenas oito unidades da Federação. No Espírito Santo, ficou a 185 votos do patamar exigido.

Em 27 de outubro, porém, o TSE aprovou um critério de arredondamento dos percentuais que permitiu à federação cumprir a exigência também no Espírito Santo. Com a decisão, o PSOL/Rede manteve o acesso ao Fundo Partidário e à propaganda partidária gratuita no rádio e na televisão.

articles.title: Fachin homologa delação de fundador da Reag, investigado no caso Master | G1
articles.standfirst: João Carlos Mansur é investigado sob suspeita de participar das fraudes do Master. Na proposta de delação, Mansur se comprometeu a apontar o caminho para os investigadores localizarem cerca de R$ 20 bilhões de Vorcaro.
articles.summary: João Carlos Mansur é investigado sob suspeita de participar das fraudes do Master. Na proposta de delação, Mansur se comprometeu a apontar o caminho para os investigadores localizarem cerca de R$ 20 bilhões de Vorcaro.
articles.body:
O presidente do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ), ministro Edson Fachin, homologou a proposta de delação premiada de João Carlos Mansur, fundador e ex-executivo da Reag, administradora de fundos de investimento investigada pelas fraudes do Banco Master .

No acordo de colaboração assinado com a Procuradoria-Geral da República (PGR) e enviado em setembro ao STF , Mansur se comprometeu a apontar o caminho para os investigadores localizarem cerca de R$ 20 bilhões de Daniel Vorcaro, ex-banqueiro preso desde março deste ano .

🎯 A delação premiada, ou colaboração premiada, é um meio de obtenção de provas nas investigações criminais. Nesse recurso, o investigado se dispõe a cooperar com o processo e a investigação. Em troca, o Estado pode dar benefícios a ele.

Além disso, Mansur se comprometeu a explicar como os fundos de investimento foram usados para lavagem de dinheiro.

João Carlos Mansur foi alvo de busca e apreensão da Polícia Federal em janeiro, na segunda fase da Operação Compliance Zero, que investiga o Banco Master .

Um acordo de delação premiada precisa ser homologado pela Justiça para passar a valer. O juiz analisa aspectos formais do acordo, como a voluntariedade do delator e a legalidade dos benefícios oferecidos.

As investigações sobre o Master estavam com o relator André Mendonça, mas desde setembro passaram para a análise de Fachin , presidente do Supremo, devido a divergências e suspeitas sobre integrantes do próprio tribunal.

A Procuradoria-Geral da República (PGR) pediu urgência na homologação da delação por causa do possível perecimento de ativos — o que significa perda ou desvalorização de ativos financeiros. Esse dinheiro pode ser usado para reparar os prejuízos causados pelos crimes investigados.

articles.title: Jessicão é alvo de ação para remoção de post por assédio eleitoral | G1
articles.standfirst: Caso condenada na ação civil pública por assédio eleitoral, deputada eleita em 2026 terá que pagar indenização de R$ 1 milhão. Jessicão informou que não foi comunicada sobre o processo até o momento.
articles.summary: Caso condenada na ação civil púbica por assédio eleitoral, terá que pagar indenização de R$ 1 milhão. Jessicão informou que não foi comunicada sobre o processo.
articles.body:
Postagem foi feita na plataforma X — Foto: Reprodução/Redes sociais

Jessica Ramos Moreno ( PL ), conhecida como Jessicão e atual vereadora de Londrina , no Norte do Paraná, é alvo de uma ação civil pública do Ministério Público do Trabalho (MPT) que determinou a remoção imediata de uma publicação feita em redes sociais em que Jessicão incita a 'demissão de petistas'. Ela foi a deputada estadual mais votada do estado, com 131.673 votos, e assume o mandato em janeiro de 2027.

A postagem foi feita pela plataforma X, anteriormente conhecida como Twitter, em 25 de outubro, depois do resultado do segundo turno das eleições presidenciais, que resultou na reeleição do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ( PT ).

Na publicação, Jessicão afirma que empresários devem demitir funcionários 'petistas', ou seja, que estejam alinhados ao Partido dos Trabalhadores (PT).

"Você tem uma empregada que é petista? Demita! Tem um funcionário que é petista? Demita! Seu barbeiro é petista? Troque de barbeiro. Amigos petistas? Demita! A porcaria do voto dele prejudica o seu negócio, prejudica a sua família e prejudica toda a sua vida! Demita o mal", escreveu Jessicão.

Para o MPT, a prática configura assédio eleitoral. Segundo o órgão, foram mais de 100 denúncias contra a vereadora por conta da publicação.

De acordo com o órgão, além dessa postagem, a vereadora terá que retirar outros conteúdos que induzam ou incitam práticas discriminatórias de acesso à relação de trabalho. A decisão também inclui que, se condenada na ação, a parlamentar terá que pagar R$ 1 milhão de danos morais coletivos, valor equivalente a R$ 1,00 por visualização da postagem.

Até a tarde desta sexta-feira (6), a publicação tinha 1 milhão de visualizações. A decisão do MPT afirma que esse alcance possui “amplo potencial de que a mensagem discriminatória atinja um incontável número de empregadores, que podem ser sentir autorizados à prática de assédio eleitoral e discriminação por convicção política”.

O valor da indenização, em caso de condenação, será destinado ao Fundo de Defesa de Direitos Difusos ou ao Fundo de Amparo ao Trabalhador ou, ainda, para entidades sociais filantrópicas.

Ao g1 , Jessicão informou em nota que não foi comunicada sobre o processo e que irá se manifestar depois de ter "conhecimento de todos os elementos", mas frisou seu compromisso com a "liberdade de expressão". Confira a nota completa abaixo .

Com 33 anos, Jessicão está no segundo mandato como vereadora de Londrina , cidade onde nasceu. É casada e mãe de dois filhos gêmeos.

Como vereadora, foi autora do projeto de lei que proibia o uso da chamada linguagem neutra em escolas e concursos da cidade. A lei foi aprovada, mas foi declarada inconstitucional pela Justiça, após manifestação do Ministério Público do Paraná (MP-PR).

Em fevereiro de 2026, a vereadora propôs um requerimento de urgência na Câmara Municipal para proibir a participação de uma atleta transexual na semifinal da Copa Brasil de Vôlei Feminino, realizada na cidade.

Na primeira disputa municipal, em 2020, Jessicão se elegeu vereadora com 2.523 votos. Na segunda, foi a mulher mais votada da cidade, com 15.057. Nas eleições de 2022, entrou na lista de suplentes para deputada federal depois de ter 33.376 votos.

Homem é denunciado por estupro de vulnerável por abordar criança que ia para a escola em Curitiba ; vítima fez sinal universal de pedido de socorro

Em nota, Jessicão informou que não deixará de se manifestar, dentro dos limites da Constituição Federal e das leis. Confira .

"Sobre a ação mencionada envolvendo meu nome, esclareço que, até o momento, não tive acesso oficial ao processo, tampouco fui formalmente comunicada de seu inteiro teor.

Assim que tiver conhecimento de todos os elementos, poderei me manifestar de maneira responsável e apresentar os esclarecimentos necessários.

Reforço meu compromisso com a liberdade de expressão, um direito fundamental garantido pela Constituição Federal e indispensável à democracia. O debate político, a manifestação de opiniões e a liberdade de pensamento precisam ser respeitados, independentemente de posições ideológicas.

Não abrirei mão do meu direito de me manifestar, sempre dentro dos limites da Constituição e das leis.

A democracia pressupõe liberdade, pluralidade de ideias e respeito ao contraditório".

articles.title: As Congress returns to Democrats, one likely casualty emerges: Trump's District of Columbia projects
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — In his first public appearance after an election that soundly repudiated his policies, President Donald Trump turned to a topic both famili...
articles.body:
The top photos of the week by AP photojournalists

WASHINGTON (AP) — In his first public appearance after an election that soundly repudiated his policies, President Donald Trump turned to a topic both familiar and, given the context, surprising: not his policies or politics but his efforts to remake pieces of the city that is the backdrop to his presidency.

Despite Trump's affinity for project management, though, with Democrats taking control of Congress, the work his administration is doing to change the physical face of the District of Columbia is sure to encounter far more roadblocks than it did for the first two years of his second term.

From the renaming of and renovation plans for the Kennedy Center to remaking a public golf course and erecting an arch 100 feet (30.48 meters) taller than the Statue of Liberty without its pedestal, Trump has been deeply involved in how D.C. looks. Democrats have voiced opposition but, in terms of power, have been in the wilderness.

The potential collision point between opposition oversight from Democrats and the Republican president's preoccupation with the projects was evident in his last message to the American public before the election — and in his first afterward, too.

Both focused to some degree on his projects. On Monday, it was the reflecting pool in front of the Lincoln Memorial ; on Wednesday, it was a tour of the under-construction White House ballroom , where he talked columns and steel beams and Corinthian designs.

The clouds of scrutiny are already gathering

Rep. Jared Huffman of California, the top Democrat on the Natural Resources Committee with jurisdiction over the Interior Department that is involved with operations at parks and federal lands, spent much of the past year probing and questioning Trump's projects, laying the groundwork for this moment.

"We've pushed back against vanity projects that seek to transform treasured public spaces into gaudy tributes to Trump. We exposed corruption, uncovered the efforts to hijack America's 250th birthday , demanded accountability, and offered a compelling alternative governing vision grounded in science, fairness, environmental responsibility, and the rule of law," Huffman said in a letter to colleagues seeking their support to be chairman.

As chairman with a strong Democratic majority, "I will ensure that the Committee's full investigative and oversight authority is leveraged to uncover wrongdoing, demand accountability, and protect the public interest," he said.

Trump has been rushing the various projects, a point Virginia Democratic Rep. Don Beyer made Thursday at a public hearing when he opposed construction of the memorial arch the president has planned in Memorial Circle directly across the Memorial Bridge from the Lincoln Memorial.

"The appropriations process beginning Jan. 3 will be controlled by Democrats. That will be one of the ways Congressman Beyer will step in," said Beyer's spokesman Aaron Fritschner.

A less appreciated impact will be the change in who names the general counsel of the House. The House Speaker has that role, presumably Rep. Hakeem Jeffries.

While Democrats have joined in lawsuits opposing the various projects, their filings don't carry the weight of Congress as the minority. "You'll see the new majority pulling back the balance of power that (House Speaker) Mike Johnson was willing to cede," Fritschner said.

A planning commission hearing for the arch featured dozens of witnesses

Beyer has already been a critic, Fritschner said, and cited other members who have signed on in amicus briefs. More than 120 witnesses were on hand for the National Capital Planning Commission meeting, which ran for 9 ½ hours late into Thursday night.

The commission gave the 250-foot (76-meter) arch its final approval on an 8-4 vote, before a federal judge stepped in before midnight to block the Trump administration from breaking ground for 14 days.

The remote, call-in commission hearing — which crashed repeatedly and was accompanied by a nearly universally negative comment section — drew witnesses who gave impassioned, three-minute comments opposing an arch they said will destroy the solemnity of nearby Arlington National Cemetery.

The Trump-appointed chairman of the commission, however, launched into a gushing appraisal of the towering monument and lauded Trump for wanting to build it.

U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan is considering a motion from three veterans and an architectural historian to stop any work until the lawsuit is resolved. A separate lawsuit filed Saturday by the District of Columbia and Virginia has been consolidated with the existing one. D.C. and Virginia have asked for a temporary restraining order, which Chutkan granted late Thursday with her 14-day delay.

At Wednesday's ballroom construction site tour, Trump spoke about the ballroom, the East Potomac Golf Links and the National Garden of American Heroes proposed for West Potomac Park and the arch. All four have been, or are currently in, litigation.

One of them, the golf course, has turned into an undertaking beyond the potential construction. U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes has said she plans to open a "formal inquiry" to investigate if attorneys for the Trump administration violated ethical boundaries during a legal dispute about that project.

Beyond the courts, Congress is now an added bulwark

Skye Perryman, president and CEO of Democracy Forward, which is representing the plaintiffs in several of the lawsuits, said the switch of control means the organizations that have filed lawsuits and challenged the administration will now be joined by Congress.

Organizations like hers will continue challenging the administration in court, she said, but "the important thing now is that the American people now have a tool that's not just in the courts."

Added Perryman: "We hope and we anticipate Congress will fulfill its constitutional duty of checking executive branch excesses." That includes hearings and investigations into funding plans and sources, she said.

Information about estimates for work on the projects has been slim, even in court, with assessments trickling out during testimony in some cases. One number, for example, revolves around the seawall at the golf course, which would exceed $300 million. Congress appropriated $257 million for the renovation of the Kennedy Center.

The White House did not respond to requests for comment.

Another area that could impact the District of Columbia is the change in governorships. Texas, Georgia, Iowa and Nevada all have Democrats coming into power as a result of Tuesday's elections. They account for more than 600 National Guard members who are part of the mobilization that Trump ordered in August 2025.

Democrats who provided troops during the celebration of the United States' 250th anniversary were roundly criticized for their participation and removed their troops and airmen months ago. Nearly 3,100 are stationed in the city now, up slightly from last month.

articles.title: El nuevo ministro de Transportes, Carlos Cuerpo, coge distancia de su predecesor, Óscar Puente: "No insulto ni provoco"
articles.standfirst: Defiende que su labor se centra en evidenciar las diferencias entre las propuestas políticas
articles.summary: Defiende que su labor se centra en evidenciar las diferencias entre las propuestas políticas
articles.body: Que la política nacional ha cambiado tras el accidente de Urda donde fallecieron 69 personas, es evidente. De hecho, se llevó por delante al ministro de Transportes Óscar Puente que dimitió de su cargo en una sesión de la Cámara Permanente y dio paso a un Carlos Cuerpo que dirige el ministerio de forma interina debido a la proximidad inminente de las elecciones generales del 29N. Un cambio que ha hecho evidente el propio Cuerpo en una entrevista en 'La Úlrima Hora', programa de la nueva cadena de televisión La Séptima, y que ha dejado claro su postura en las confrontaciones políticas. Lo ha hecho a través de una autodefinición de cómo es su forma de hacer política: "No insulto, ni entro en ningún tipo de provocación, entre otras cosas porque creo que no me hace falta. Aparte de que cada uno tiene una manera de ser distinta". Unas palabras que ya marcan distancias de su predecesor. Profundizando en el papel de la sociedad ante las urnas, ha querido poner en valor el criterio de los electores de cara a las próximas citas con la democracia. Según su análisis, "los ciudadanos somos suficientemente maduros como para ver cuál es la actuación, cuál es la actitud de cada una de las opciones políticas que se presentan a las elecciones del día 29 de noviembre y qué es lo que están proponiendo". Asimismo, ha apuntado a la necesidad de centrar el debate público en los asuntos verdaderamente transcendentales para el día a día. En este sentido, ha recordado que es vital debatir sobre "la gestión en los temas esenciales, véase infraestructuras, estado del bienestar, sanidad, educación, empleo, los modelos que se contraponen". Para concluir, ha zanjado cualquier duda sobre su labor diaria afirmando con firmeza su diferencia con la anterior manera de gestionar: "Mi trabajo no está en crispar, mi trabajo está en evidenciar la diferencia que hay entre los modelos, este es un modelo que protege y que además fomenta la propia prosperidad, el crecimiento compartido de nuestra economía y ahí es donde queremos estar".

articles.title: Reporter's Notebook: How midterms may change the House impeachment equation for Hegseth
articles.summary: Thomas Massie plans to reintroduce articles of impeachment against Pete Hegseth next week, and post-midterm GOP math could work against the Pentagon chief.
articles.body:
Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., plans to reintroduce articles of impeachment for Pentagon Chief Pete Hegseth next week. The chances are increasingly high that the House could in fact impeach Hegseth.

Massie tried to impeach Hegseth before the midterms. But the House adjourned a day early in September, nixing Massie's effort. House Speaker Mike Johnson , R-La., condemned the effort by Massie. But insisted that he didn't send members home early because of fear that the House had the votes to impeach Hegseth.

So Massie's articles of impeachment expired. But he will reintroduce them next week. Under the rules, the House must consider them within two days.

It's possible the House could move to table the articles, or send them to committee, euthanizing the effort. But a growing number of House Republicans have grumbled about Hegseth. Any effort to dismiss the articles in the House might not work.

All Democrats are likely to vote to impeach. There are some Republicans who have said privately they'd like to impeach. Now, after the midterms, you have more Republicans hoping to build distance between themselves and President Trump. Moreover, the war in Iran contributed directly to the GOP's thumping. So even more Republicans may be willing to impeach. Finally, the GOP may have attendance problems. Members who lost — or were shocked that they lost — might not show up. In other words, there may be more Democrats in the House next week than Republicans.

Don't forget that some Republicans are now looking for a scapegoat after the election.

A simple majority is necessary to impeach.

Then the House would send the articles of impeachment to the Senate.

Under Senate rules of impeachment, the Senate must at least receive and consider the articles. But it could move quickly to dismiss. That's what happened when the Senate considered articles of impeachment for former Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas a few years ago. The bona fide "trial" part of the process never happened where the Senate heard arguments, listened to witnesses and took evidence.

It takes a simple majority to dismiss such articles. Again, this could happen under a Republican-controlled Senate. But how might outgoing Sens. John Cornyn, R-Texas, Thom Tillis, R-N.C., and Bill Cassidy, R-La., vote?

That's to say nothing of Sens. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, John Curtis, R-Alaska, Todd Young ,R-Ind., and others.

It takes a two-thirds vote to convict and remove in a Senate impeachment trial.

In addition, unlikely legislation, articles of impeachment carry over into the new Congress. Would a new Democratically-controlled Senate want to get bogged down in an impeachment trial from the start? Especially when new Democrats want to vote on affordability and health care?

Or, would a Democratic Senate embrace the idea of a full-blown impeachment trial for Hegseth – especially since the execution of the war in Iran seems to be one of the main reasons for this week's electoral shellacking?

articles.title: ‘Voter apathy’ toward Hyde-Smith could be factor in Mississippi Senate race: Professor
articles.summary: A Mississippi political science professor said voters seemed to be “really enthusiastic” about Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom, but when it comes to...
articles.body:
A Mississippi political science professor said voters seemed to be "really enthusiastic" about Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom, but when it comes to his opponent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R), "there was a lot of voter apathy."

"Colom's a really high-quality candidate," Aaron Hitefield, assistant professor in the Mississippi State University Department of Political Science and Public Administration, said during an appearance on NewsNation.

"Voters seemed really enthusiastic about him … when you compare that to Cindy Hyde-Smith, the current incumbent, there was a lot of voter apathy," Hitefield added. "I think you see that in the results currently."

The Senate race in the historically red-leaning state remains uncalled as Colom maintains a lead of a little more than 2,000 votes, according to The Hill's partner Decision Desk HQ . In the neck and neck battle for a seat in the U.S. Senate, the Democrat is leading by just 0.2 percentage points.

Mississippi Republican Party Chair Mike Hurst told the press Thursday that if "the laws are followed and the voters spoke, that is it and Mississippi Republicans will accept that ."

"There is no election denying going on here," he said.

The ballots are still being received in the Magnolia State, which allows mail ballots to be counted and received up to five business days after the election as long as they are postmarked by Election Day.

Attorneys for Hyde-Smith recently demanded in a letter sent to the election commissioners in all 82 Mississippi counties that election officials separate the affidavit ballots, document their disposition and preserve "all associated materials."

An attorney for Colom , in a letter sent to county election commissioners Thursday, said the Republicans' demands "have no basis in Mississippi law."

"If you depart from ordinary election procedures as you have been asked to do, you will violate Mississippi voters' rights and Mississippi election law," the lawyer wrote in the letter.

By current tally, the Democrats will hold 54 Senate seats and, with Mississippi and Alaska still undecided, that number could grow to 56.

articles.title: Sununu blames Trump for GOP midterm shellacking
articles.summary: Senate Republican candidate John Sununu says President Trump deserves much of the blame for Republicans’ blowout losses in Tuesday’s election, which will giv...
articles.body:
Senate Republican candidate John Sununu says President Trump deserves much of the blame for Republicans' blowout losses in Tuesday's election, which will give Democrats their biggest Senate and House majorities in years.

Sununu in an interview with SiriusXM's "The John Kasich Show" said Trump's inability to end the months-long conflict with Iran and his failure to "drain the swamp" as he pledged to do in the 2024 campaign cost Republican candidates dearly.

"Now it seems like he or his family is on every transaction and deal that goes on in Washington," Sununu said. "Those two things, I think, caused people to say, 'You know, I just can't vote for a Republican while he's still in office.'"

Sununu lost the New Hampshire Senate race to Rep. Chris Pappas (D-N.H.) by 13 percentage points despite Republican hopes that they had a good chance of stealing the Democratic-held seat.

Sununu represented New Hampshire in the U.S. Senate from 2003 to 2009, when he was defeated by retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.)

Trump, however, has blamed GOP candidates for not doing a good enough job of promoting themselves and has argued that he would have carried many of them to victory if he were on the ballot as he was two years ago.

"I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!" Trump posted on Truth Social on Tuesday night as the election returns showed a blue wave sweeping across the country.

Vice President Vance on Wednesday cited the war with Iran as the biggest reason why Republicans fared so poorly in this year's midterm election.

"The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," Vance wrote in a social media post.

"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest," Vance argued.

"But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there," he said.

But some Republican strategists are acknowledging privately that Democrats' attacks on Trump's family business dealings and other allegations of corruption in the Trump administration also moved voters.

Sununu told "The John Kasich Show" that future Republican presidential aspirants such as Vance will suffer political fallout after Republicans' disastrous showing in the midterms.

"The closer you are to the president, the worse a night it was for you as a potential presidential candidate," he said.

Sununu predicted that Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) would explore a presidential run in the next election cycle to boost her political brand.

"Some people run for president because they really think they can win and that they'll be a great leader and an important leader for the country. Some people run for president because it's good for their business model," he said.

"And I put AOC in the latter category. So, will she test the waters and go through the kabuki? One hundred percent. Because her business model is built around followers and attention," he added.

articles.title: Louisiana Republicans confront voter frustration after midterm losses
articles.summary: (The Center Square) — Louisiana Republicans are questioning President Donald Trump’s handling of the conflict with Iran, immigration enforcement and the risi...
articles.body:
(The Center Square) — Louisiana Republicans are questioning President Donald Trump's handling of the conflict with Iran, immigration enforcement and the rising cost of living after a Democratic midterm wave nearly cost the GOP a U.S. Senate seat in one of the country's most reliably Republican states.

Several Republican state legislators interviewed by The Center Square described a party struggling to retain the enthusiasm of working-class voters who helped return Trump to the White House in 2024. Some blamed the administration's policies for worsening economic pressures, while others pointed to Republican voters staying home.

The criticism comes after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress and captured major statewide offices across the country, including in traditionally Republican strongholds like Texas and Kansas, where Republicans suffered historic defeats.

Louisiana narrowly avoided a similar upset. Republican Julia Letlow defeated Democrat Jamie Davis by approximately 26,000 votes, a strikingly close result in a state Trump carried by nearly 22 percentage points two years earlier.

Although Republicans retained Louisiana's U.S. Senate seat, two congressional races remain undecided. Republicans Gabe Firment and Blake Miguez will compete in December runoffs in the 5th and 6th Congressional Districts, respectively.

The Republican Party has already endorsed both, as have current U.S. Reps. Mike Johnson and Steve Scalise, as well as Governor Landry.

Front and center in Tuesday's election was Trump's ongoing conflict with Iran, which has driven up the costs of gasoline, transportation and consumer goods, adding to the financial pressures already facing American households.

"I think that has taken a real toll," state Sen. Franklin Foil, R-Baton Rouge, said in an interview. "And there doesn't appear to be an end game in sight."

State Rep. Chuck Owen, R-Rosepine, has been "proven wrong" on the conflict with Iran. "I'm puzzled as to why we haven't wrapped it up any sooner."

Democrats in Louisiana and across the country seized on that frustration, making affordability a central issue in their campaigns and portraying Republicans as increasingly disconnected from the economic concerns of ordinary voters.

Only two years ago, the Republican Party was able to seize on the same frustration and galvanize voters unhappy with then-President Joe Biden.

"They felt inspired by a mission of greatness, American prosperity," state Sen. Heather Cloud, R-Turkey Creek said. "I think over time, we've watched them be picked off. They've lost their inspiration. They've lost their their motivation, and I guess the party to some degree has lost its charisma."

Letlow received approximately 745,000 votes Tuesday, about 455,000 fewer than Trump did in 2024. Overall, roughly 540,000 fewer Louisianans cast ballots than in the presidential election two years earlier.

"When the Louisiana conservative base is energized, it pulls in 1.2 million votes," Owen said. "No one else comes close to that. I don't think John Bel [Edwards] ever got to 800,000."

Following Tuesday's Democratic sweep, Cloud took to Facebook, lamenting the economic pressures facing ordinary Americans, citing the rising cost of living and the prolonged conflict with Iran.

But Cloud also criticized Trump's aggressive immigration enforcement, arguing that the administration is "failing to distinguish between criminals and hardworking, taxpaying immigrant families."

Cloud said that Trump has done well to secure the border, but that the administration's deportation campaign has alienated Hispanic immigrants who have lived in the country for years, sometimes decades, and have been working toward citizenship.

Many, she said, have no criminal history and are productive members of their communities, yet "they were being rounded up" and given no option but to leave the country, sometimes separating families in the process.

State House Majority Leader Michael Echols, himself fresh off an election defeat, agreed with Cloud that there need to be better pathways for legal immigration, specifically for agriculture and high-demand jobs without Americans to fill them. Echols, a Republican from Monroe, encouraged Congress to pass a law to offer those pathways.

Echols said national Republicans need to refocus on the financial pressures facing Americans, particularly high fuel prices, health care costs and government regulations. He also called for reforms to the health insurance industry, arguing that insurers and pharmacy benefit managers have driven up costs for consumers.

In Louisiana, Echols said lawmakers should require large data center developers to cover the costs of electricity infrastructure and improvements to surrounding communities, rather than leaving those expenses to residents.

The concerns reflect a broader challenge facing Louisiana Republicans.

The state has attracted billions of dollars in announced industrial investments under Gov. Jeff Landry, while education rankings have improved and violent crime has declined. But those developments have done little to resolve the everyday affordability concerns that legislators say dominated Tuesday's election.

For the Republican Party, the immediate challenge is ensuring those frustrations don't translate into another defeat when voters return to the polls in December.

"I couldn't believe how bad of a beating we got," Louisiana Republican Party Chairman Derek Babcock told The Center Square. "I feel good about these two congressional runoffs. But the Democrats are energized. And if our people don't show up, we're in trouble. We could lose it."

articles.title: Midterm returns show bad news for progressive Democrats
articles.summary: The 2026 midterm election showed that leftists like Abdul El-Sayed significantly underperformed compared to more moderate Democrats.
articles.body:
The 2026 midterm election showed that leftists like Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed — and even candidates who have been affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America — can win in competitive areas of the country, under the right circumstances.

But it also showed the danger of nominating candidates like them.

Many of them won, but they also often ran worse than other Democrats — and even further behind some of the party's most moderate candidates.

The results clearly illustrate that nominating more moderate candidates remains the most fruitful path to winning swing seats and states. And they suggest candidates like El-Sayed could cost Democrats in less-wavey elections.

While the party previously nominated these kinds of candidates in dark-blue districts, it nominated El-Sayed in the Michigan Senate race and a DSA member in a swing congressional district in that state. It also nominated left-wing candidates for Senate in Florida and Minnesota, and in several House districts that had voted for President Donald Trump in 2024 — including in California, Maine, Montana, Pennsylvania and Tennessee .

Bernie Sanders-backed Senate candidates were the worst performers

This trend was most evident in the Senate results.

In fact, in key races, the four candidates most aligned with the party's left flank — and endorsed by influential democratic socialist Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont — accounted for the four worst performances, compared to 2024.

They were Maine Senator-elect Troy Jackson (half a point worse than Kamala Harris, as things stand), Minnesota Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan (5.9 points better), El-Sayed (8.4 ponts better) and Florida Senate candidate Angie Nixon (10.2 points better).

The average Democratic Senate candidate in key races ran sixteen points better than Harris did in 2024.

These candidates are different flavors of leftists, for sure. Nixon is an actual DSA member who joined in June. El-Sayed is not a democratic socialist and has called himself a capitalist, but he clearly comes from the left wing of the party, and many prominent Democrats feared that nominating him would cost them the seat even in a strong Democratic environment. Both Jackson and Flanagan are also pretty liberal, with Flanagan having defeated a more moderate primary opponent in Rep. Angie Craig.

All four of these candidates also ran worse than the Democratic gubernatorial candidates running on the same ballots.

These candidates account for 4 of the 5 candidates that Sanders endorsed . The fifth, Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts, won easily in blue Massachusetts. But he also notched one of the party's worst performances compared to Harris' numbers in his state, beating her 2024 margin by just 5.8 points.

In contrast to how these candidates performed, we saw many of the more moderate Democratic candidates notch some of the biggest over -performances.

North Carolina Senator-elect Roy Cooper over-performed Harris by 23.2 points. Mississippi Senate candidate Scott Colom, who ran as a pro-law enforcement moderate , is currently over-performing by 23.1 points and could pull the upset of the election cycle over GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. Senator-elect Adam Hamilton in Kansas, Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia and Senator-elect Josh Turek in Iowa ran 21.1, 20.2 and 17.2 points better than Harris, respectively.

Some of the other biggest over-performances came from candidates with less moderate (and even rather "woke") pasts — but who clearly ran as moderates this time. That includes Senator-elect James Talarico in Texas (25.7 points better than Harris) and Senator-elect Dr. Annie Andrews in South Carolina (21.9 points better).

It's true that Democrats won nearly all of these races, regardless. But given these results, it's valid to wonder if they could have also won the Florida race — which Nixon lost by about three points — if they didn't have a nominee affiliated with the DSA.

The results in the battle for the House told a similar tale, though the differences are less stark.

Pollster G. Elliott Morris of Strength In Numbers ran the numbers in all races and found that progressives and members of the Congressional Progressive Caucus over-performed Harris by an average of 12.2 points. That was compared to 14.1 points for members of the more-moderate New Democrat Coalition, and 15.4 points for moderate-to-conservative Blue Dog Democrats.

Curiously, Morris found that DSA candidates actually over-performed by even more — an average of 16.5 points.

But that's from a very small sample size of just seven candidates. And they were generally running in very blue districts where, yes, being far to the left might be an asset.

The picture in more-competitive districts suggests far-left candidates could have — and likely did — cost Democrats.

Perhaps the biggest win for the left was in Michigan's 7th District, where Democratic Rep.-elect William Lawrence won a swing seat. Lawrence was a member of the DSA when he won his primary, though he left the group in the general election. His win, like El-Sayed's, could be read to prove that far-left candidates can win swing districts.

But Lawrence only narrowly won, and he only over-performed Harris by a relatively meager 4.3 points. That's one of the smallest over-performances in the House.

Also telling: In Maine's 2nd District, Sanders-backed state Auditor Matt Dunlap over-performed Harris by just 8.1 points and lost.

The result was particularly striking because retiring moderate Democratic Rep. Jared Golden had managed to keep the Trump-supporting district in Democratic hands in far-less-favorable environments in recent years. Dunlap defeated a more-moderate candidate backed by the national Democratic Party in the primary.

The district apparently will now be the bluest one that Democrats won't represent in the House — and the party can blame a Sanders-backed candidate.

Left-wing Democrats appear to have performed about on-par with other Democrats in districts like Colorado's 8th, Montana's 1st and Pennsylvania's 7th. Rep.-elect Randy Villegas also won a swing district in California's 22nd district, but it's too early to compare his margin to 2024 (more than 40% of the vote is yet to be counted as of Friday morning).

There was one left-wing candidate who significantly over-performed but came up short in a pretty red district. It was Democrat Justin J. Pearson, whom you might remember from when he was expelled from the Tennessee state House in 2023. He lost by just one point in a district Trump had carried by 21, even after campaigning with New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

Still, that was the exception to the rule.

There's a clear lesson for Democrats looking at these election results: It's preferable to run moderates — and avoid far-left candidates — in battleground areas. After all, huge blue waves like this also tend to be the exception, not the rule.

articles.title: Dems pivot from ‘affordability’ pitch to DHS probe threats after midterm wins
articles.summary: Robert Garcia and other Democrats campaigned on affordability but pivoted to subpoenas and Trump investigations after winning, Fox News Digital found.
articles.body:
Several prominent Democrats who ran on an "affordability" message were largely silent when pressed by Fox News Digital on their sudden pivot to foreshadowing investigations into the Trump administration, including in many cases its immigration enforcement efforts.

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is poised to lead the House Oversight Committee, responded to Democrats' win Tuesday with a statement: "Lawyer Up" , despite having pledged to prioritize household costs alongside government accountability.

Garcia told CNN before the election that "Democratic priorities" would be lowering the cost of "gas, groceries, the mortgage, the rent," alongside combating government corruption.

In response to a request for comment, a representative for Garcia shared a tweet he posted Wednesday, after his Tuesday "lawyer up" warning, that referenced affordability:

"People can't afford gas, groceries, and rent because Donald Trump and his family are ripping off the American people and enriching themselves. Taking on corruption is about making life more affordable for working families," Garcia said in the tweet.

Before the election, "Squad" Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., wrote in a PBS-Chicago voters guide that there is "no question that the rising cost of living is the number one issue" for a " working people's agenda ."

After the election, however, her tone appeared to change:

"Noem, Markwayne, Miller, Homan, Bovino, what's up? Clear your schedule," Ramirez said .

Several respondents pushed back, including one of her stated targets, former Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino.

"Honey, slow your totalitarian roll," Bovino responded on X. "Citizens don't answer to communists in this country as much as you seem to believe that."

Bovino went on to suggest Ramirez instead relax with a bottle of whiskey from a brand the former immigration official launched upon retirement.

Other respondents also pointed out that Ramirez' post-election missive didn't mention her affordability priority:

"Notice nothing about how she is going to help her constituents but 'get Trump'," said one.

"So, you guys never really gave a s--- about affordability," added former Energy Department staffer Matt van Swol.

Rep. Analilia Mejia, D-N.J., who now represents the longtime Republican-held seat of former Rep. Rodney Frelinghuysen, made both affordability and immigration policy part of her campaign message.

"We're going to toss out subpoenas like Mardi Gras beads," Mejia's first X post Wednesday read.

Rep. Tony Wied, R-Wis., responded it showed Democrats "have no plans to make life better for you," eliciting a response from Mejia in which she dubbed him "Mr. Weird" and only then mentioned an "economy that works for" Americans.

In April, Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., released a lengthy statement announcing a "New Affordability Agenda" and highlighting her role on the Congressional Progressive Caucus' "Lowering Costs Task Force."

On Election Night, Ansari posted : "Thank you Mr. President. Our thank-you will come in January with subpoenas." An ensuing tweet called for the impeachment of War Secretary Pete Hegseth.

On Wednesday, Ansari ultimately posted a policy-related pledge to curtail AI.

Sen. Edward Markey, D-Mass., stated during the midterms that his priorities were " groceries, gas prices energy costs " and the like.

However, his post-election missive remarking on how many "new forests" will need planting for "all of the subpoenas we'll be printing," instead signaled a priority to investigate tech executives like Elon Musk .

"Affordability," quipped former Virginia Del. Nick Freitas, R-Culpeper, in a reply.

Ramirez, Mejia, Markey and Ansari did not respond to requests for comment on their apparent pivots. Garcia's representative responded by providing his subsequent post on affordability. Both Garcia and Ramirez had previously identified government accountability and immigration oversight, respectively, as priorities, but their immediate post-election statements emphasized investigations rather than the affordability measures they had highlighted on the campaign trail.

DHS appeared to take the newfound priority in stride in comments to Fox News Digital.

"It is unfortunate that Democrats are more interested in political shenanigans than in governing," said DHS' top attorney James Percival.

"Rest assured, however, that we are well prepared to deal with this nonsense so Secretary Mullin can continue focusing on protecting the homeland," the counsel said.

A Justice Department spokesperson echoed Percival, saying the agency is "not afraid of threats from Democrats" and assured its staff has followed the law.

"It is no surprise that rather than focus on bringing down costs for Americans, Democrats in Congress are picking up where their weaponization efforts left off when they were last in power," the spokesperson said.

Meanwhile, the White House told Fox News Digital that Trump remains willing to work with Democrats on issues they can collaborate on to help "hardworking Americans."

"If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical-left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people," spokeswoman Lauren Bis said.

Immigration hawks signaled preparations for what Democrats foreshadowed.

The Mass Deportation Coalition , whose leaders have been critical of Biden-era open-border policies and have asserted that the Trump administration has not done enough on the issue in some areas, told Fox News Digital they are prepared to defend officials amid the onslaught.

"We know what's coming," said Mass Deportation Coalition leader Mike Howell. "A lot of people are going to be cashing-out and charging patriots expensive legal fees to the most vulnerable."

"We have been through this before and are ready to sacrifice for the patriots who are targeted by weaponized harassment."

Former House Oversight Committee counsel and immigration judge Andrew Arthur said Congress has the prerogative to investigate DHS' work but added that it may not be what Americans are looking for as a priority.

Citing Ramirez' mention of Border Czar Tom Homan , Arthur noted that the onetime Obama official long held "positive" ratings from Republicans and Democrats.

"He was commonly viewed as the guy who came in and cleaned things up after Noem left, got things a little bit better. So that's probably not going to be a terribly popular thing," he said.

"This isn't really affordability but anything that shows waste in government technically goes to affordability and it all depends on how willing the media is to accept that talking point," said Arthur, now at the Center for Immigration Studies.

Arthur said DHS can largely proceed as usual with its previously established funding while any investigations take place, adding that much of what Mullin and Trump have done already falls under established law that Congress itself passed.

Referencing the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952, Arthur said that, short of "amending the law itself – which they can't do if [Trump] vetoes it" Democrats can probe and try to paint the agency in a "bad light" over ICE-involved shootings and similar incidents, but that their larger agenda would be buttressed by the INA.

A 2026 whitepaper by Federal Reserve Bank researchers found elevated "unauthorized" immigration contributed to rising housing costs between 2021 and 2024, estimating that the influx increased home prices by 6.6% and rents by 4.3% in the average metropolitan area.

The researchers attributed the increases to additional housing demand that was not matched by sufficient new construction, lending indirect empirical support to arguments that illegal immigration can have adverse effects on key affordability metrics.

articles.title: Three Justice Department officials, including man behind Trump’s ‘grand conspiracy’ probe, resign since brutal midterm losses
articles.summary: Three high-profile officials have resigned from the Justice Department in the days since the midterms, including Jason Reding Quiñones, the senior federal pr...
articles.body:
Three high-profile officials have resigned from the Justice Department in the days since the midterms , including Jason Reding Quiñones, the senior federal prosecutor who led a sprawling investigation into President Donald Trump's political foes.

Quiñones resigned from his position as the US Attorney in Southern Florida under pressure from department leadership, despite his willingness to pursue some of the most controversial investigations desired by the president, according to sources familiar with the matter.

John Eisenberg, who led the department's National Security Division, also announced his resignation Friday, and Harmeet Dhillon left her post as the head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division on Thursday.

The turnover at the Justice Department had been expected for weeks for a variety of reasons. With the anticipated midterm outcome, some officials are expected to return to lucrative law firm jobs while the second Trump administration still has two years remaining in office.

With Democrats now poised to have oversight control and launch investigations, some top Justice Department officials believe the firebrands inside the Justice Department could be more of a liability.

Blanche has sought to try to restore control over the department, with some officials like Quiñones and Dhillon viewed as causing problems by making high-profile promises that they couldn't deliver on. Democrats aren't likely to lose interest in investigating the actions of Dhillon and Quiñones despite their departure.

The resignations could be a challenge for the administration, which is expected to have trouble confirming new officials with a Democratic Senate. But the president could install acting leaders to do the job for the rest of his term.

The man behind a sprawling 'grand conspiracy probe

Attorney General Todd Blanche announced Quiñones departure in a social media post Friday, saying that the department is "grateful for Jason's leadership."

Quiñones being pushed out in Miami deals what may be the final blow to the Justice Department's ongoing effort prosecute a wide swath of Trump's perceived political enemies as part of a so-called "grand conspiracy."

During his year-long tenure, Quiñones' office won one of the most consequential criminal indictments brought by the Trump Justice Department: The indictment against former Cuban President Raúl Castro.

But other antics left him on the outs with department leadership. Quiñones was behind the effort to use a grand jury in Fort Pierce, Florida, to pursue investigations of former government officials who were involved in probes of Trump and his campaign from 2016 to 2024.

He promised that his office could bring the case within months against former government officials who were involved in probes of Trump and his campaign from 2016 to 2024, top Justice officials blamed him when those plans failed to materialize.

And Quiñones frequently traveled outside his district, often to Washington, DC, which only reminded top DOJ officials of his failure to produce a big case he had promised.

In the Miami US Attorney's Office on Friday, Blanche's announcement came as a shock. Many were in the dark about Quiñones seeming rapid fall from grace, according to people familiar with matter.

articles.title: Mary Peltola Appears Likely To Defeat Both Dan Sullivans in Alaska's Senate Race
articles.summary: Meanwhile, President Donald Trump impotently called for the state to just give Sullivan all the other votes and declare him the winner.
articles.body:
Days after the midterm elections, one of the only national races still left to be resolved is the U.S. Senate race in Alaska. As of this writing, with about three-fourths of the votes tallied, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan trails Democratic challenger Mary Peltola by just over 600 votes—three tenths of a percentage point—with the two remaining candidates trailing further behind, with just a couple of percentage points each.

The race received intense scrutiny in its final days after it came to light that the Peltola campaign and other Democrats recruited current fourth-place finisher Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. specifically to siphon votes from Republicans confused about which Dan Sullivan to vote for.

President Donald Trump called for Peltola and the other Sullivan to be criminally prosecuted. The Department of Justice sued , asking the state to set aside ballots that picked the non-incumbent Sullivan. (A federal judge dismissed the lawsuit earlier this week.)

There are still plenty of votes left to count, but it appears unlikely for Sullivan—either one—to pull out a victory. Not only that, it seems like he's losing fair and square.

For its general elections, Alaska uses a ranked-choice ballot, listing up to four candidates for each office regardless of party affiliation. Voters rank the candidates in order of preference. In the event that nobody receives an outright majority when the votes are counted, the lowest performer is eliminated, and all of their ballots are retallied and assigned to their second choices.

Besides that, even just collecting and processing ballots in such a large and mostly rural state means it'll take a while. The state must count all ballots by November 18—15 days after Election Day—and it has another seven days to certify the results.

But the state released preliminary results this week on the approximately 215,000 votes it had collected, which suggests people who voted for the other Sullivan did so not out of confusion, but to vote against the incumbent.

"Mr. Sullivan might not even claw back half of a point in ranked-choice tabulation, which would not be enough to overcome Ms. Peltola's expected advantage," reports The New York Times . "One reason Mr. Sullivan doesn't fare better is that more of the voters who backed the other Dan Sullivan…ranked Ms. Peltola as their second choice rather than Mr. Sullivan."

The Times analyzed the data available, which includes all but about 10,000 ballots that could not be scanned electronically and must be counted by hand.

Only about four percent of ballots ranked someone other than Peltola or Sullivan first. Of those who picked the other Sullivan, over one-third left the rest blank, nearly 30 percent picked Peltola second, and 16 percent and 18 percent picked the incumbent Sullivan and fellow Republican Gerald Heikes, respectively.

This suggests that at least 16 percent, and perhaps as many as 34 percent, of voters followed the senator's advice to just list all the candidates other than Peltola and let the process sort it out.

It also indicates nearly three in 10 voters who picked the spoiler Sullivan actually did intend to vote for Peltola, and ranked her second.

Of the voters who picked Heikes first, 36 percent picked Sullivan second, and a nearly identical amount left the rest blank; 14 percent picked the other Sullivan, while 12 percent chose Peltola.

Of course, there is the matter of the 36 percent who picked the other Sullivan and nobody else—were those protest votes, or confused voters?

Thankfully, there is reason to think the Peltola campaign's dirty trick did not actually sway the results: "Even if all the voters who voted for Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. and did not rank a second choice at all had actually intended to vote for the incumbent," the Times added, "he would only gain about one percentage point in vote margin—an increase that would not offset Ms. Peltola's expected gains from uncounted mail vote."

Of course, that hasn't stopped Trump from fulminating over the results.

"The vote totals for the Fake Dan Sullivan, plus the other 'slug' that the Dems put on the Ballot, should be immediately given to the REAL Dan Sullivan, and the Election is over - He easily wins," the president wrote on Truth Social . "There is no other fair solution!"

Why stop there? Why not also give Sullivan the 695 write-in votes? While we're at it, why not just give him Peltola's votes too and declare a unanimous victory?

This impotent posturing is Trump's natural response when he comes up short in elections.

After he won the 2016 election but lost the popular vote, Trump complained that if not for "the millions of people who voted illegally," he would have won both. (There was no evidence for this claim.)

Then, before the 2020 election, he reportedly indicated that he planned to just declare victory before all the votes were counted—which he then did , as state totals were trending away from him.

Even in this campaign cycle when he's not on the ballot, Trump's administration has tried to meddle in states' counting processes: Before Election Day, his Department of Justice tried to force Alaska to segregate all ballots that voted for the other Dan Sullivan, in order to conduct some sort of "investigation" into whether each voter actually meant to vote for the incumbent senator.

And this week, attorneys for Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R–Miss.) sent a letter to election officials in Mississippi, where Democratic challenger Scott Colom currently leads Hyde-Smith by about two-tenths of a percentage point.

In that race, there are estimated to be between 15,000 and 20,000 provisional ballots left to be counted. Hyde-Smith's attorneys wrote "to demand the immediate separation, secure custody, and preservation" of all provisional ballots, in the event of a lawsuit challenging the results.

As Madeline Nguyen of Mississippi Today reported in April, Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson contracted with Experian to verify voters' eligibility even as the company warned that it couldn't guarantee the data was reliable. As a result, thousands were likely removed from the voter rolls erroneously and had to cast provisional ballots.

Both before and since the election, Trump complained about the Alaska Senate race, saying the Peltola campaign had committed fraud and must be punished. Ultimately, it looks like Peltola will win not because of malfeasance, but because voters simply liked her opponent less.
