articles.title: White House won’t comment on where Trump’s many midterm promises stand — including those $5k checks
articles.summary: President Donald Trump dangled the promise of $5,000 checks to every American adult before the midterm elections, with a key stipulation: Republicans had to...
articles.body:
President Donald Trump dangled the promise of $5,000 checks to every American adult before the midterm elections, with a key stipulation: Republicans had to win.

And it wasn't the only such promise he made, all tied to Republican wins and several in states critical to Senate control. During his extensive October rally tour, he vowed to: settle water contamination lawsuits in North Carolina, invest in a drug manufacturing facility in Kentucky, make a fuel commonly used by farmers more readily available in Kansas and Iowa and to continue federal help in Alaska.

Now that a blue wave decisively washed out Republican control of Congress, the White House isn't commenting on those promises. Asked about updates to the $5,000 checks and other Trump vows, spokesperson Matthew Middleton responded vaguely, touting past accomplishments.

"Moving forward, the President will work with anyone willing to advance solutions that strengthen our economy. We hope Democrats will put the American people first and join us in that effort," Middleton said in a statement.

Pressed on whether Trump has officially scrapped the idea for the $5,000 checks, the White House did not reply.

Trump himself hasn't publicly commented or been asked about any of the promises since the election, including in two public appearances touting the White House ballroom and designating the Cabinet room and Oval Office national landmarks. He's also had several phone interviews this week after it was clear Republicans were losing control of both chambers of Congress.

His comments at rallies that Republicans had to win in November to get their checks were highly criticized at the time, as many doubted he would follow through — even if Republicans did win — and critics dubbed the promise as an unsubtle attempt at bribing the electorate.

"Our country is doing so well under Republican leadership that only I can make this promise here. This might be, for some people, the most important thing I'll say," Trump said in Kalispell, Montana. "If Republicans can win the House of Representatives and the US Senate, I am going to give all adult citizens of the United States of America, $5,000 a year, and only a Republican president can do that because Democrats can't."

Even GOP lawmakers were critical of the promise, with outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis calling it a "gimmick" that wouldn't solve real problems.

Fox News anchor Laura Ingraham also asked Trump in September why he wouldn't just give the checks right away. He responded "they can't" and then criticized Democrats again.

The president frequently tried to portray his vows as something he could only accomplish if Republicans still had majorities in Congress next year. He didn't address why he hadn't accomplished those goals in the past two years, or whether he would in the next couple of months, while Republicans still control both chambers.

And sometimes his claims — that a pot of critical money would seemingly evaporate under Democratic control — didn't make sense.

One of those promises involved tying a Republican victory to settlement claims for water contamination at Camp Lejeune .

"If we win the House and the Senate, I am directing the Department of Justice to settle all remaining legitimate claims as soon as possible and get it off the books and get it finished. It's gone on for years," Trump said in Greenville, North Carolina, on October 20.

"If we don't win, there's no money," he continued. "If we do win, you're getting it. It's going to be finally over with — that nightmare that's been going on for so many years."

At the time, a White House spokesperson said, "President Trump is the only one who can bring closure and justice to victims of water contamination at Camp Lejeune" and pointed to his full comments, where he said that the administration had been "fighting for our great veterans" and delivered $1 billion in cash settlements so far.

While the White House and Trump said he wants to work with Democrats, the administration has previously withheld disaster aid from Democratic-led states and admitted in July that it canceled clean-energy grants in states that voted for Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential campaign.

Trump had joked on the campaign trail that he wouldn't give North Carolina hurricane disaster funding unless his Senate pick, Michael Whatley, won.

"Now, if Michael loses, I'm not sending it," Trump said, adding, "No, I'm only kidding."

About a month later, Vice President JD Vance announced at his own rally for Whatley that the administration was sending an additional $858 million in disaster relief to the state.

articles.title: Democrats win the Arizona House, Senate and governor’s office for the first time since 1966
articles.summary: PHOENIX (AP) — Democrats in Arizona won control of both legislative chambers and retained the governor's office, giving the party its first trifecta in the s...
articles.body:
PHOENIX (AP) — Democrats in Arizona won control of both legislative chambers and retained the governor's office, giving the party its first trifecta in the state since 1966 as Democrats made major gains nationwide in this week's elections and took control of both chambers of Congress .

In her first term, Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs had vetoed more than 540 measures passed by the Republican-led Legislature on policies including taxes, immigration and voting laws. Hobbs has said she's looking to address water issues and affordability, and take on fraud and abuse in the state's school voucher program.

The Associated Press called enough legislative races to confirm that both chambers flipped on Friday. The news organization calls races individually and it can take several days after voting, depending on when election officials tally the votes and how close the elections are. There have not been major disputes or disruptions this year.

In Arizona, Republicans have held the House for 60 years and the Senate since the early 1990s.

Overall, Democrats took full control — both statehouse chambers and governors' offices — in at least six states where they previously shared power with Republicans. Besides Arizona, those wins were in the battleground states of Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, Nevada and Wisconsin.

The flips weren't just in states that are normally competitive. Democrats won control of the Texas House, which Republicans have held since 2003, and elected Gina Hinojosa as the state's first Democratic governor since George W. Bush ousted Ann Richards in 1994. Republicans held onto the state Senate.

Democrats also flipped the lower chambers of the legislatures in Maine and North Carolina and both chambers in New Hampshire, where Republican Kelly Ayotte was reelected. The count could grow as results are tallied in additional states.

The National Council of State Legislatures says it's likely to end up as the election with the most legislative seats and chambers changing parties since the 2010 election, when Republicans took over governments across the country amid the Great Recession.

Democrats will also hold the governor's office in at least 28 states. Results are still pending in Alaska and Kansas.

articles.title: Trump names Stephen Miller his new chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles
articles.summary: President Donald Trump has turned to MAGA favorite Stephen Miller to lead the White House after Republicans got trounced in Tuesday’s midterm elections, losing both chambers of Congress by wide margins.
articles.body: President Donald Trump has turned to MAGA favorite Stephen Miller to lead the White House after Republicans got trounced in Tuesday’s midterm elections, losing both chambers of Congress by wide margins. Trump announced the change at the top on Truth Social Friday afternoon, with Miller, his deputy chief of staff, taking over chief of staff duties from Susie Wiles on Monday. Wiles submitted her resignation Thursday night, according to a White House official. The shift from Wiles, a longtime establishment figure in Florida and national political circles, to Miller, the hard-charging architect of the president’s mass-deportation campaign, sends a signal to a fractured Republican Party that Trump intends to strengthen ties to the MAGA base in his final two years in office. It also portends an even more contentious relationship with Democrats in Congress, who have demonized Miller for years. “Miller knows the key issues and is a true believer — and he knows the ecosystem around the issues,” said Steve Bannon, a former senior Trump aide and host of “The War Room” podcast. “Stephen gets parachuted in and takes immediate control.” On a recent phone call with an ally, Trump praised Miller as an aide who gets things done and doesn’t just tell him what he wants to hear. The ally said that Miller will be combative with Congress, particularly when it comes to any investigations Democrats point toward the administration. “When the president says, ‘Do this,’ Stephen will do it, and he’ll leave bodies behind doing it,” the ally said. Miller did not immediately respond to a request for comment on how his promotion would change the operation and direction of the White House. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is widely expected to become speaker in January, called for Miller to be fired, not promoted. “Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands,” Jeffries wrote on X. “His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor. Fire him today.” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said the news showed that Trump “learned nothing from his historic defeat.” “Stephen Miller is the architect of the most barbaric, inhumane policies of this administration. Trump couldn’t have made a worse choice,” he wrote on X. “Our Democratic majorities will fight him every step of the way.” Miller, who worked as a senior aide on Trump’s first campaign and has been with him ever since, is known within the White House as the ultimate loyalist to the president and a harsh taskmaster to underlings. In May 2025, for example, Miller berated and threatened to fire Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials over what he viewed as paltry numbers of arrests and deportations of undocumented immigrants. He demanded that they figure out how to detain 3,000 people per day. A familiar presence in right-wing media as an ardent advocate for the hard-line immigration policies he developed for Trump, Miller lowered his public profile after federal agents killed American citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis in January. In the immediate aftermath of Pretti’s shooting, while facts were still being gathered, Miller erroneously tweeted that Pretti was a “domestic terrorist” who tried “to assassinate federal law enforcement.” He later said that the White House had received bad information from Customs and Border Protection. The decision to hand the White House keys to a hard-nosed MAGA warrior comes just three days after voters soundly rejected a Trump second-term record that centered on base-minded policies, from tariffs and deportations to slashing government programs. Most midterm voters said Trump’s immigration enforcement actions have gone too far, according to initial results from the NBC News Exit Poll. That was the view of 57% of voters, while 23% said they have been about right and 21% said they have not gone far enough. While Democrats were energized and independents shifted away from Republicans, many GOP voters stayed home Tuesday. The move to Miller fits with Trump’s general mien of indifference to the anger of voters. He spent Election Day and the day after talking about pet renovation projects that are peripheral to the affordability concerns voters said they want addressed. The decision appeared to be made quickly. In mid-October, Trump told NBC News that Wiles would “be there until the end,” following speculation that the president might be considering a replacement. Wiles, a 69-year-old cancer survivor, has been in the job longer than any of the other four chiefs of staff who served in Trump’s first term. Trump said Friday Wiles has “done an outstanding job” and “will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!” Moments later, Wiles wrote in a post on X that Friday would be her last day as chief of staff. “Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First,” she wrote. “While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will.” For some, the switch could be understood as a natural byproduct of the midterm results. “The president loves her and I think he really did mean what he said about wanting her to stay, but there are those in his base who don’t trust her, don’t think she is part of the MAGA movement and are going to blame her for the midterms,” said one former Trump administration official. “This was a nod to those people in a moment when he will need his remaining political base intense as Democrats start coming for everyone.” Or, as a person close to the White House put it, “It definitely sends the right message to the base.” Miller, who served as an aide to conservative Sen. Jeff Sessions, R-Ala., and in other roles on Capitol Hill before joining Trump’s 2016 campaign, spent years accumulating influence with the president. In early 2025, an ally described him as “untouchable” in the White House. He understands and executes on Trump’s vision, and he has demonstrated an absolutist version of loyalty to the man and his agenda, people familiar with their relationship say. Mark Bednar, a Republican strategist who worked in Congress when Miller was an aide there, said the choice will serve Trump well. “Even since his days on Capitol Hill, Stephen has been a both long-view strategist and also a tireless, meticulous tactician,” Bednar said. “When you combine that skill-set with his understanding of President Trump’s policy goals, that is an incredible combination for a chief of staff. He will serve well in this role for President Trump.”

articles.title: Trump names Stephen Miller new White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles
articles.summary: Susie Wiles served 21 months as Trump's longest-serving chief of staff across both terms, departing after Republicans lost the House and Senate. Trump announced Stephen Miller will take on the role.
articles.body: President Donald Trump named Stephen Miller his new White House chief of staff, calling him one of his "most trusted advisors" on Friday. Miller will ascend to the role on Monday, officially replacing Susie Wiles, who Trump said will be moving to his political operation. "I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!" Trump wrote. Moments after Trump's announcement, Wiles issued a statement of her own. "Today is my last day as White House Chief of Staff," Wiles said. HEGSETH'S FUTURE DRAWS OMINOUS PREDICTIONS FROM INSIDERS AFTER GOP LOSSES, BUT TRUMP ISN'T BUDGING YET "Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First," she added. "More than anything, I’m grateful for the extraordinary people I’ve had the privilege of working alongside. While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will." Trump told reporters Friday, before departing on Marine One. that Wiles did a "great job." "I think [she's] done a very good job. Great job. But I just wanted to make this even been great. We got to make. We've got to make those. So sometimes in life, we have to make [moves]," said Trump. In March, Wiles announced she had been diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer upon early detection and received a strong prognosis. Six months later, in September, she shared that she was cancer free. "With grit, determination, faith and the support of extraordinary people, it is possible to fight this disease while continuing to embrace the work, relationships and sense of purpose that make you who you are," Wile wrote in a USA Today op-ed in September. "For me, that means serving my president and my country. I will always be grateful to President Donald Trump for the kindness and compassion while I was undergoing treatment." TRUMP PLEDGES TO VETO 'INSANE' DEM BILLS, PINPOINTS ISSUE PARTIALLY TO BLAME FOR REPUBLICAN LOSSES The Friday announcement came after Republicans lost control of both the House and Senate in the midterm elections, dealing a major blow to President Donald Trump after the war with Iran and persistent affordability concerns loomed large over elections, as voters weighed the economic toll of the conflict. A White House official told Fox News Digital the decision was "very amicable" and Wiles handed her resignation on Thursday night. "A great pick. He has the trust of millions of Americans who understand that reversing mass migration is the crisis of our time," an administration official told Fox News Digital. Wiles worked on Trump’s 2016 and 2020 campaigns, making history as the first woman to serve as chief of staff. She is a longtime Trump ally, first throwing her support behind him in 2015 when she became the Trump campaign's co-chairwoman in Florida. "As a card-carrying member of the G.O.P. establishment, many thought my full-throated endorsement of the Trump candidacy was ill-advised — even crazy," Wiles told the New York Times in a rare public statement back in 2016. Wiles has served in her role for 21 months, making her Trump’s longest-serving chief of staff across both of his terms. Trump cycled through four chiefs of staff during his first term, with John Kelly serving the longest—about 17 months. 'POD SAVE AMERICA' HOSTS CALL DEMOCRATIC PARTY'S MIDTERM WINS 'THE END OF THE TRUMP ERA' She has been dubbed the "Ice Maiden" by Trump, which he noted in his 2024 victory speech, for her hard-nosed approach to handling business. Wiles was seen as Trump’s behind-the-scenes enforcer, sitting in on high-level meetings and standing by his side at events, while Wiles rarely spoke directly to the public. Current and former Trump administration officials posted on social media to thank Wiles and congratulate Miller. "Very grateful to Susie for her friendship and service to the president and our country. Stephen Miller is an amazing patriot and will do great things. Congrats to him on a well deserved promotion," wrote Vice President Vance. "Stephen Miller is a Trump OG, someone who has been with the President since the very beginning. There is no bigger advocate for the Trump agenda than Stephen, and he will help the Administration deliver on monumental victories for the rest of this historic second term," wrote White House communication director Steven Cheung. "A huge thank you to Susie Wiles for her incredible service to our nation! She’s a rockstar and will no doubt continue working to make our country great. Looking forward to continuing our work with my good friend Stephen Miller as Chief. Together we’ve reduced crime to historic levels, enhanced public safety throughout our communities, and continue to root out the massive fraud that has taken advantage of American taxpayers. We’re not slowing down," wrote Attorney General Todd Blanche. Wiles played a central role in engineering Trump's return to the White House, earning a reputation as one of his most trusted political strategists. But her transition from campaign mastermind to White House chief of staff has also brought its share of challenges, with a few high-profile controversies drawing scrutiny during her tenure. Wiles faced scrutiny during her tenure over several controversies, including her involvement in a Signal group chat in which Secretary of War Pete Hegseth shared sensitive details about impending U.S. military strikes against Houthi militants in Yemen. The chat inadvertently included the editor-in-chief of The Atlantic, who later exposed the discussions. The administration denied that classified information had been shared. articles.title: Trump names Stephen Miller as new chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles
articles.summary: Miller, considered the architect of Trump's hard-line immigration policy, will move into the role on Monday.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has named Stephen Miller, the architect of his hardline immigration policy, as his new chief of staff following historic losses in the US midterm elections.

Miller replaces Susie Wiles, who submitted her resignation after Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress, delivering a blow to the prospects for Trump's agenda in his final two years in the White House.

Speaking to reporters, Trump said Wiles had "done a very good job", but "we've got to make moves sometimes".

Miller, a Trump loyalist and deputy chief of staff who served as a senior adviser during his first administration, is set to take on the new role on Monday.

One of Trump's closest aides, Miller stuck by the president following his 2020 election defeat and followed Trump back into power last year.

Wiles gave her resignation to Trump on Thursday night, a US official told CBS News, the BBC's media partner. Three sources told CBS she quit because of the election losses.

Trump said in a statement that Wiles would be moved to the "Trump Political Operation". He told reporters that Miller "gets it, very good politically".

Wiles said being on Trump's team was "the honor of a lifetime".

"I'm so proud to have been a part of what we've accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First," she said. "While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will."

It was unclear if her deputies would remain at the White House.

Wiles, 69, is seen as among the most powerful figures in the Trump administration and someone particularly close to the US president.

Asked last month whether Wiles could be replaced soon, Trump said there was "zero chance".

"Susie is here and she's gonna be here for a long time," he said.

Wiles recently battled cancer, announcing in September, six months after her diagnosis, that she was in remission.

Wiles is not the only high-profile Trump official to leave this week following the midterm elections, which have prompted a reckoning among Republicans about how to address voters' rebuke of Trump's agenda.

Several justice department officials have also resigned, including John Eisenberg, the head of the department's National Security Division, and Jason Reding Quiñones, who was known for enforcing conspiracy probes into officials investigating Trump's handling of classified documents.

Democrats took to social media to criticise Trump's new pick, accusing him of doubling down despite voters' anger with his party's agenda.

Democratic Congressman Robert Garcia, who would lead the House Oversight Committee after Democrats take control of the chamber, said he would continue to investigate Miller and his "misconduct".

"Stephen Miller is the architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids that have terrorized our communities and kidnapped and killed American citizens and immigrant families," he said, referencing US Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Democratic House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said Miller was "a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands".

"His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor," he said.

Trump's communications director Steven Cheung called Miller "someone who has been with the President since the very beginning".

"There is no bigger advocate for the Trump agenda than Stephen, and he will help the Administration deliver on monumental victories for the rest of this historic second term," he said.

articles.title: Reporter's Notebook: A user’s manual to upcoming leadership elections in the House and Senate
articles.summary: Capitol Hill leadership elections pit Hakeem Jeffries against progressive dissent, while Steve Scalise and Jim Jordan battle for GOP minority leader.
articles.body: Internal party House and Senate leadership elections are some of the most fascinating exercises that unfold on Capitol Hill. Both House and Senate Democrats and House and Senate Republicans will choose their leaders in the coming days. And the changes are going to be seismic. But not everyone is on board with heir apparent leaders. That’s what makes this process so intriguing. However, there are only two rules in leadership elections: You can’t beat someone with no one. And, perhaps more importantly, it’s about the math. PROGRESSIVES FUME AT HAKEEM JEFFRIES FOR SAYING DEMOCRATS WON'T 'GET EVEN' WITH TRUMP There are some progressives and DSA-affiliated Democrats who will be House Members next year who want someone other than House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y. Who? Well, no one has said. Again, you can’t beat someone with no one. And, frankly, it’s hard to believe that Democrats would not elect the first Black speaker of the House. But drill down on the math. For the sake of argument, let’s say Democrats have 260 House seats in the new Congress. First, Democrats must tap a nominee for speaker in their caucus. That needs a simple majority. So, surely Jeffries will score at least 131 votes in a private ballot for speaker. The speaker of the House is the constitutional officer for the legislative branch of government, much like the president is for the executive branch and the chief justice of the United States for the judicial branch. Thus, the ENTIRE House votes for speaker when it convenes the new Congress at noon on Jan. 3. There are 435 members. If all members cast ballots, Jeffries simply needs 218. Jeffries could lose 40 votes or so and still prevail. So, that is not going to happen. It might not even lose more than a couple votes, frankly. Now let’s look at the GOP and their case for minority leader. House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., is running against Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio. If Democrats have 260 seats, Republicans would have 175. All INCOMING House Republicans (including non-voting delegates from U.S. territories) are allowed to vote in CONFERENCE. The selection of minority leader does NOT go before the entire House like speaker. So, the winning candidate only needs a simple majority. That would be 88. The same for the race between House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., and Rep. August Pfluger, R-Texas, for minority whip. MIKE JOHNSON'S NO 2 LAUNCHES GOP TAKEOVER BID AS HOUSE FALLS TO DEMOCRATS The Senate Democratic Caucus and Republican Conference work much the same way as the House. A simple majority wins for majority leader in the Democratic Caucus and minority leader in the Republican Conference. However, the selection of Senate majority leader is not a vote that plays out on the floor. The concept of "Senate majority leader" has only been around since the early 20th century and is not mentioned in the Constitution. Remember what we said about the House speaker being the head of this branch of government. It would be hard to envision a scenario where Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., would not become majority leader after Democrats flipped the Senate in a beatdown. First, who else is running? Well, Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, is popular among Senate Democrats. But he’s running for majority whip to succeed retiring Senate Minority Whip Dick Durbin, D-Ill. One could see Democrats defaulting to Schatz if something happens with Schumer. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., has said he wants to look at his options and has endorsed Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., for majority leader. But Van Hollen isn’t running. Sen.-elect Annie Andrews, D-S.C., told colleague Bret Baier she wants a "generational change" in leadership. Sen.-elect Troy Jackson, D-Maine, and Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton, D-Kan., both said they would oppose Schumer. FIRST MUSLIM SENATOR, FIRST BLACK FEMALE GOVERNOR: 2026 MIDTERM ELECTION RESULTS MAKE HISTORY But again, you can’t beat someone with no one. Here’s the math: Let’s say Democrats do win Mississippi and Alaska, giving them 56 senators who caucus with the Democrats. All Schumer needs is 29 Democrats to support him in the Caucus, and he’s the next majority leader. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP There has not been as much rumbling about the future of Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D. Heretofore, President Trump has not called for new leadership in the Senate. But Senate Republicans would choose Thune or anyone else on a secret ballot in the Senate GOP Conference. A simple majority would win. If Republicans are down to 44 seats, the winner would just need 23 votes.

articles.title: Trump elevates Stephen Miller after midterms disaster
articles.summary: One House Republican told Semafor the move was “a horrible decision.”
articles.body:
President Donald Trump on Friday announced that Stephen Miller — the architect of his aggressive immigration enforcement agenda — will succeed Susie Wiles as the next White House chief of staff.

The decision to shake up White House leadership was led by Trump, a source close to the White House told Semafor, adding that the president placed some of the blame on her for the party's catastrophic midterm showing.

His choice of Miller sends an undeniable message of defiance to the incoming Democratic congressional majorities. The current deputy chief of staff for policy is widely disliked by Democrats and even some Republicans who see his agenda as partly to blame for their dismal performance in the midterm elections.

Indiana Republican Rep. Marlin Stutzman, who had called for Miller's firing after the midterms, said elevating him to chief of staff was a "horrible decision."

Miller's ascension will cool the prospects of an immigration deal in the next Congress, despite some hopes to find common ground in divided government. A former GOP congressional aide himself, Miller was instrumental in killing a bipartisan immigration deal in 2018.

Questions have swirled in the administration for months about whether Wiles, Trump's longest-serving top aide, would remain as chief of staff for all four years. Long seen as uniquely qualified in minimizing infighting and drama, Wiles faced a series of blistering pre-election headlines that were described to Semafor as an effort to oust her; Trump stood by her at the time.

One person familiar with the situation described Wiles' exit as initiated by Trump following his anger over the midterms, but also something she was willing to set in motion.

"She said, 'Let me make this easy on you, I am going to resign,'" the person said.

Miller counts his share of backers on the right, and his elevation will deliver a boost to Trump's faithful after the resounding blow of Tuesday's election. He will begin his new role on Monday, the president said.

"Hiring Stephen sends the right message to the base and he is probably the best possible person to help rebuild our fractured coalition. He is a wartime consigliere," the person close to the White House said.

White House communications director Steven Cheung said in a social media post that Miller "will help the Administration deliver on monumental victories for the rest of this historic second term."

Trump said Wiles, who recently worked through successful treatment for breast cancer, will be moving to his outside political operation. She submitted her resignation on Thursday, a White House official said.

Two senior Justice Department officials are also leaving their posts, per Reuters .

When Wiles was away from the White House, a Trump Cabinet member pitched the president on a nominee to lead ICE, Semafor reported — and the pick was later withdrawn.

articles.title: Sen. Chris Murphy discharged from hospital after stroke
articles.summary: The Connecticut Democrat will spend “several weeks at a rehabilitation center” after being discharged from The Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore, Maryland.
articles.body: Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., was discharged from the Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore, after suffering what his doctor called a “small hemorrhagic stroke” last weekend, his office announced Friday. Murphy, 53, said in a written statement that he will be spending “several weeks at a rehabilitation center” after being discharged from the hospital. “Last Saturday afternoon, I felt something was not right with my body and called 911 out of an abundance of caution, and I’m glad I did,” Murphy said. “I was diagnosed with a small bleed in the thalamus region of my brain.” Calling the medical event “a scary experience for me and my family,” Murphy said he is “staying engaged with my team and colleagues remotely” as he works toward his recovery. “My staff continues to carry out our legislative priorities, serve constituents, and ensure the work of my office continues uninterrupted,” he said. Dr. Jose Suarez, Johns Hopkins’ chief of neurosciences critical care, said in a statement provided by the senator’s office that Murphy “has shown tremendous progress, and at the current rate of improvement, we expect that he will make a full recovery following rehabilitation.” A hemorrhagic stroke happens when a blood vessel in the brain ruptures and bleeds. Some of the symptoms include headaches, dizziness, trouble understanding or speaking, one-sided weakness, neck stiffness and fainting, according to the Cleveland Clinic. It’s unclear what led to the senator’s stroke. Murphy’s chief of staff, Allison Herwitt, said in a statement Sunday that the senator had experienced symptoms a day earlier, when he “started experiencing numbness in his arm while at his son’s hockey game.” “He was taken to a local hospital, where it was discovered he had experienced a stroke,” Herwitt said. “He was transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring and is responding well to treatment.” She added that the senator was awake and alert, and the doctors were encouraged by his progress. Murphy was not up for re-election Tuesday, but he had been actively campaigning for fellow Democrats. He’s considered a potential 2028 presidential contender. Murphy is the deputy secretary of the Senate Democratic Caucus, a role that could change in the new Congress with his party set to take the majority early next year. He sits on the Appropriations, Foreign Relations, and Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions committees. He served in the House from 2007 to 2013 before becoming a senator that year. Three other Democratic senators have had strokes in recent years, including Ben Ray Luján of New Mexico, Chris Van Hollen of Maryland and John Fetterman of Pennsylvania.

articles.title: Houston mayor bolts early from ICE cooperation after blue wave crashes in Texas
articles.summary: Houston Mayor John Whitmire bars police from notifying ICE during nonviolent stops despite defeated Texas Republican Gov. Greg Abbott's order.
articles.body: The Democratic mayor of America's fourth-largest city is reversing course on cooperation with federal immigration authorities despite an executive order from defeated Texas Republican Gov. Greg Abbott that threatened the loss of millions in state funding for noncompliance. The Lone Star State swung blue for the first time since its new senator-elect, James Talarico, was born, and Houston Mayor John Whitmire wasted no time Friday announcing new restrictions on cooperation with ICE. Whitmire told The New York Times that city police are not permitted to notify ICE if they encounter an illegal immigrant in "nonviolent contacts" like traffic stops or minor offenses. 'WE DIDN'T EXPECT THIS': TEXAS DEMOCRATS STUNNED AS BLUE WAVE TOPPLES GOP STRONGHOLD "If they’re charged with a new crime, we’ll let ICE know as we get them to the jailhouse," he told the paper Friday. Abbott lost his bid for a fourth term Tuesday, and Talarico flipped one of the state’s Senate seats blue for the first time since Clinton Treasury Secretary Lloyd Bentsen won his final re-election bid in 1988 — seven months before the current senator-elect was born. Texas’ most recent Democratic governor, Ann Richards, the mother of former longtime Planned Parenthood president Cecile Richards, was elected shortly thereafter in 1990. Whitmire did not respond to a request for comment but signaled to the Times that he made the decision at least in part because Abbott’s order requiring DHS contact caused "anxiety" among Houstonians. In a statement put out Friday afternoon, Whitmire said, "I have signed an executive order directing HPD to no longer contact ICE for nonviolent offenses, helping reduce fear in our communities. Thank you to Chief Diaz, our state and local leaders for their collaboration. A step toward building a stronger Houston. Let’s Go to Work." He also acknowledged Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa won’t take office until January but characterized his decision as "responsible" and "more effective policy." A DHS spokesperson responded to Whitmire's move in comments to Fox News Digital. "We remain disappointed that sanctuary politicians seek to limit cooperation with ICE, as our law enforcement are simply fulfilling their sworn duties to serve and protect our communities," the spokesperson said. "Partnerships with law enforcement are critical to having the resources we need to arrest criminal illegal aliens across the country. Seven of the top 10 safest cities in the United States cooperate with ICE. When politicians bar local law enforcement from working with DHS, our law enforcement officers have a more visible presence so that we can find and apprehend the criminals let out of jails and back into communities. The spokesperson pointed to some recent criminal illegal aliens captured by ICE in Houston – including Alexander Montano of Cuba, convicted of willful homicide, burglary and forced entry into a residence. Vietnamese national Ding Nguyen, also convicted of homicide, along with Guatemalan national Julio Camey, convicted of sex offense against a child, were also mentioned by the spokesperson. "You write a citation or you warn them, and they go about their way. No contact with [ICE] over nonviolent, non-jailable offenses," Whitmire told the AP. A previous policy enacted in March by Whitmire and Police Chief Noe Diaz stipulated that if a background check revealed an immigration-related warrant, a sergeant would be called to oversee ICE involvement, according to Houston’s FOX affiliate. The policy also said that if ICE could not make it to the stop within half an hour, the subject would be released. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER The Houston City Council subsequently approved an ordinance in April limiting how long officers could detain individuals while awaiting ICE agents, but Whitmire backed revisions after Abbott threatened to withhold more than $100 million in state funding and then-Attorney General Ken Paxton launched an investigation into the city's immigration policies. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The revised policy restored greater discretion for officers to contact ICE and wait for federal agents during encounters involving civil immigration warrants. Whitmire's latest announcement would instead limit such notifications to encounters involving jailable offenses, marking a return to the restrictions city lawmakers initially sought.

articles.title: In Republican collapse, Colorado military town elects Democrat for the first time
articles.summary: (In paragraph 12, corrects title to "vice chairman" from "chairman;" In paragraphs 24 and 25, corrects name to "Ries" from "Trei")  COLORADO SPRINGS, Colorad...
articles.body:
In Republican collapse, a Colorado military town elects first ever Democrat

(In paragraph 12, corrects title to "vice chairman" from "chairman;" In paragraphs 24 and 25, corrects name to "Ries" from "Trei")

COLORADO SPRINGS, Colorado, Nov 6 (Reuters) - Colorado Springs, a military town and global center for Christian evangelism, has sent a Republican to Washington every election since its US House of Representatives district was created in 1970.

The ‌victory of Jessica Killin, an Army veteran who was among dozens of Democrats who flipped a seat this week, is one of the starkest examples of how the party built ‌its resounding win on affordability issues, demographics and candidates, one district at a time.

In an area with five military installations, where soldiers pack fast-food restaurants at lunchtime, Killin's triumph relied on votes of veterans, service members and their families, who represent about a ​third of the population, and for whom the war in Iran is personal. A soldier deployed from the city's Fort Carson US Army base was among the first Americans to die in the conflict.

Killin, a first-time candidate, said her win was a repudiation of Republican incumbent Jeff Crank's support for President Donald Trump and underscored voters' frustrations with the Iran war, tariffs and the Jeffrey Epstein scandal.

A supporter who canvassed for her found immigration also was on the minds of Latinos in a district where the population of metropolitan Colorado Springs more than doubled to around 782,000 in the last four decades, bringing greater ethnic diversity and a younger, more ‌highly educated electorate.

"I am resolved to make the history that really matters, ⁠combating horrific corruption and chaos that we are all honestly sick of in Washington, DC," Killin, a former US Army paratrooper and aide to ex-second gentleman Doug Emhoff, told reporters on Thursday.

Crank had tried to portray Killin as an outsider.

"We cannot let our community turn into Denver or Boulder," Crank posted on social media last week, ⁠referring to the two Democratic-controlled cities to the north.

Killin targeted centrist and left-leaning residents in the state's second-largest city, and her hometown, who in the past three presidential cycles abandoned both major parties, swelling unaffiliated voters by nearly half to 53% of the electorate in El Paso County, according to county data.

In a metropolitan area where more than 200 space, aerospace, cybersecurity, and defense companies employ around 111,000 people, and account for over 40% of the local economy, Killin hammered ​Crank's ​support of Trump's "reckless" war in Iran and argued that Congress needed to reclaim its war-powers authority.

Karl Schneider, 57, a ​former US special forces officer and ex-vice chairman of the El Paso Republican Party, ‌backed Killin to rein in a presidency he sees as militarily out of control.

"Donald Trump is a clear and present danger to the United States of America, our republic, and I think to the rest of the world," said Schneider, an executive at an AI cybersecurity advisory firm who served as a US Army Green Beret.

For Republican voter Rick Wood, 67, Crank failed to help tackle high gas and grocery prices and tied himself too closely to Trump, whose approval rating is near a career low of 32%, according to a Reuters/Ipsos national poll.

"They ran on Trump's coattails," said Wood, a US Air Force veteran.

Some Republicans interviewed by Reuters in the district that is home to the Focus on the Family evangelical organization were stunned by the blue wave, saying they feared the country would descend into communism, echoing warnings from Trump ‌about the recent rise of left-wing Democratic candidates.

Politics professor Sara Hagedorn saw Killin, and other Democrats who won in former Republican ​strongholds, as a possible return to the fiscally responsible "Blue Dog" Democrats of the 1990s and early 2000s who worked across ​party lines.

"She has a real opportunity here to be a real moderate or independent voice within ​the Democratic Party," said Hagedorn, who teaches at the University of Colorado, Colorado Springs.

Killin's campaign coffers swelled after the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee listed the district as "in ‌play" in February, the first time the committee had targeted the area.

Bruce Barron, ​65, a former Republican congressional aide, canvassed for Killin in ​southeast Colorado Springs where the school district has around 54% Hispanic students and many of the Black community live.

"Every Hispanic I talked to, it resonates with them, the concern about Hispanics not being safe under the Trump administration," said Barron.

Killin's campaign outraised Crank's by nearly two to one with $5.6 million in funds.

She deployed over 400 volunteers to knock on over 100,000 doors while hosting ​around 150 events to meet voters, according to the campaign.

As Kyle Ries, ‌40, canvassed for Killin in south Colorado Springs, where American flags fly outside many homes and fuel-hungry pickups stand in driveways, he met conservatives willing to support Killin after ​they saw Crank back a war that has stoked energy prices.

"This is a candidate that this district has never seen before," Ries, an IT professional, said of Killin.

(Reporting by ​Andrew Hay in Colorado Springs and Brad Brooks in Longmont. Editing by Donna Bryson and Alistair Bell)

articles.title: Rubio will venture to France on first post-midterm foreign trip to face questions on Trump policies
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — Secretary of State Marco Rubio will make his first international trip since the midterm elections that dealt Republicans a severe blow and...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Secretary of State Marco Rubio will make his first international trip since the midterm elections that dealt Republicans a severe blow and raised questions about how the Trump administration will respond after policies like the Iran war helped Democrats seize control of Congress .

The State Department said Friday that Rubio would leave this weekend to attend a Group of 7 foreign ministers meeting in France. He will have plenty of opportunities to explain whether President Donald Trump will adjust his often-aggressive approach to both allies and foes in the aftermath of massive Republican losses in Tuesday's vote.

In a terse statement, the department said Rubio would use the meeting to "advance American interests in engagements with his G7 counterparts." The top U.S. diplomat is seen by many as presenting a gentler side to Trump's approach , but there has been speculation — that he and aides have vehemently denied — that he might choose to leave the administration early to prepare for a 2028 presidential run .

The G7 meetings on Monday and Tuesday follow a larger diplomatic gathering that Rubio hosted in Atlanta just last weekend for G20 foreign ministers — a meeting that produced little in the way of consensus on any of the major issues the world is confronting. The Atlanta meeting, which included Russia and China, ended without a joint communique and instead a chairman's statement from Rubio.

The G7, which comprises the world's biggest industrialized democracies rather than the 20 largest global economies, is made up entirely of U.S. allies — Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy and Japan. Yet the differences that prevented broad agreements in Atlanta will likely again confound top diplomats in Paris, especially on global security.

In Paris, the foreign ministers will again confront a number of unresolved world crises, including the Iran and Russia-Ukraine wars as well as deteriorating energy and food security. Already the French have signaled that this meeting also will not produce a joint communique.

The French hosts, who have invited Brazil, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Ukraine to participate in some of the discussions, have numerous priorities, including Ukraine, Iran and freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea. The French also are looking to address the broader Middle East — including Israel, the West Bank, Gaza, Lebanon and Syria — Africa, the Indo-Pacific and China, Venezuela, Cuba and Haiti.

They also will convene a meeting on artificial intelligence and a separate session on support for Ukraine, according to the French foreign ministry.

Trump and his administration have rattled the nerves of its G7 partners on issues like support for Ukraine, NATO and defense spending as well as trade and tariffs, the Iran war and opposition to the International Criminal Court . All of the G7 members — except Japan, which has a separate treaty alliance with the U.S. — are in NATO.

To the consternation of Europe, Trump has scaled back U.S. military assistance to Ukraine as it defends itself from Russia and repeatedly suggested that America might not come to the defense of another NATO member under attack unless all allies step up their defense spending. He also has proposed reducing the U.S. military footprint in Europe , which has been a constant reassurance for the continent since World War II.

The American military presence also plays a role in the administration's battle to dismantle the ICC , the world's first war crimes tribunal to which all G7 members but the U.S. belong. The Trump administration has imposed severe sanctions on the ICC and a number of its employees, while next year it could add penalties on governments, companies and individuals that do business with the court.

The European Union is considering what's called a "blocking statute" that would protect EU institutions from U.S. secondary sanctions. It's a step the Trump administration has said would be hostile and have potential consequences for relations with the United States.

articles.title: Democrats' big midterm wins could change how we elect the next president
articles.summary: A compact between states might give Democrats the power to prevent candidates from winning the White House without winning the popular vote — if they choose...
articles.body:
Could this year's big blue midterm wave transform how America elects its next president? Now that Democrats have won complete control of governor's mansions and both legislative chambers in five battleground states — Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin, Nevada and Arizona — there is a chance that the Electoral College, as we know it, could soon become a thing of the past.

That isn't speculation. In fact, the plan is already in motion. Over the last two decades, 18 states and Washington, D.C., have formally agreed to award all of their electoral votes to whichever presidential ticket wins the most votes nationwide, regardless of the outcome in their own state or district. Until now, this legal agreement — official name: the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact (NPVIC) — hasn't taken effect because the jurisdictions that have joined it only control 222 total electoral votes, which falls short of the 270 required to activate the compact (and elect a president).

But what if you add Pennsylvania (19 electoral votes), Michigan (15), Arizona (11), Wisconsin (10) and Nevada (6) to the list? That gets you to 283 (assuming that all of them join and the compact survives potential constitutional challenges).

Since Election Day, the Democratic shift in statehouses across the country has been overshadowed by the massive Democratic shift on Capitol Hill . But as the dust settles, attention is turning toward a new possibility: that a handful of states might suddenly have the power to ensure that whoever wins the national popular vote in 2028 will also win the presidency (which hasn't always been the case ).

"The time is right," Carrie Rheingans, a Democrat in the Michigan House of Representatives, told the New York Times this week . "This blue tsunami is really going to help push this forward across the whole nation."

"National popular vote will be something that we'll prioritize early in the session," added Kelda Roys, a Democratic state lawmaker in Wisconsin.

Here's everything you need to know about the national popular vote compact — and its chances of taking effect.

How does the Electoral College currently work?

The Electoral College is a system of indirect democracy in which the winner of the U.S. presidential election is determined not by the combined number of votes a candidate has earned across all states — aka the "popular vote" — but rather by the number of "electoral votes" they've amassed by winning in individual states.

With minor exceptions, the candidate who gets the most votes in a particular state on Election Day is awarded all of that state's electoral votes, which match the number of senators and representatives it sends to Congress. Whichever presidential ticket secures a majority of electoral votes — that is, 270 — wins.

Due to the winner-take-all nature of the Electoral College, candidates tend not to campaign in states that consistently vote Democratic (blue states) or Republican (red states). Instead, they focus on the small number of states (known as swing states, battleground states, toss-up states or purple states) that could go one way or the other.

The Founding Fathers established the Electoral College in the Constitution. Some of them wanted qualified citizens to elect the president by popular vote; others wanted Congress to elect the president. The Electoral College was the compromise they landed on.

Today's Electoral College system evolved over time as individual states passed their own winner-take-all laws. But the Founders never specified how electors — the ones who cast the electoral votes — would be appointed. Instead, the Constitution explicitly delegates that power to the states themselves, saying they can choose their electors "in such Manner as the Legislature thereof may direct." National popular vote advocates argue that this clause gives state lawmakers " a built-in way to reform the system ."

How could the national popular vote compact change America's presidential elections?

Prior to the 20th century, three presidents won the White House without winning the popular vote: John Quincy Adams in 1824, Rutherford B. Hayes in 1876 and Benjamin Harrison in 1888. But the idea for a national popular vote compact only started to gain traction among scholars after George W. Bush lost the popular vote in 2000 and wound up in the White House anyway. Sixteen years later, Trump's popular-vote loss to Hillary Clinton — by a margin of nearly 3 million ballots — added more fuel to the fire.

The Bush and Trump victories also polarized the issue, making Democrats more open to the idea of reform — and Republicans more opposed (in general).

The NPVIC was introduced in 2006 by John Koza , a computer scientist and former Democratic elector who co-invented the lottery scratchcard. The idea is simple. First, individual states agree to award all of their electoral votes to the winner of the national popular vote. When enough states agree — that is, enough states with a combined total of at least 270 electoral votes — then the compact will take effect and the candidate who earns the most popular votes nationwide will be guaranteed enough electoral votes to win the White House. No constitutional amendment required.

National popular vote proponents say that their plan will completely change the way candidates campaign for (and even govern as) president. Rather than lavishing all their time, energy and resources on a small handful of swing states, aspiring commanders in chief would in theory have to cater to voters everywhere in hopes of maximizing their nationwide vote tally.

In April 2007, Maryland became the first state to sign on. Ten more jurisdictions followed suit before the 2016 election (California, Hawaii, Illinois, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island, Vermont, Washington and the District of Columbia), with another eight joining the compact after Trump became president (Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Maine, Minnesota, New Mexico, Oregon and Virginia).

Republican-led chambers have adopted the NPVIC in New York (2011), Oklahoma (2014) and Arizona (2016) — but generally, Democrats have needed complete statehouse control to enact it into law.

Which is where Democrats' shiny new trifectas in Pennsylvania, Michigan, Arizona, Wisconsin and Nevada come into play.

According to the Times, "lawmakers in key states said on Thursday that they had already begun having conversations this week about introducing legislation to join the agreement in the next session, and were hopeful that they would succeed ahead of 2028."

But hopeful doesn't mean certain. One of the new trifecta states, Michigan, failed to get over the line during its previous Democratic trifecta, from 2023 to 2024 — and Nevada fell short in 2019 when its then-Democratic governor vetoed the compact amid fears it could diminish his small state's outsized influence over presidential elections.

Virginia became the most recent state to join the compact after Democrats there won a trifecta in 2025. Republicans called the move an " unconstitutional assault on our democracy ," arguing it undermines the influence of Virginia voters.

One major question is whether lawmakers will prioritize the national popular vote after campaigning in 2026 on more visceral issues like lowering the cost of living. "Time will tell," Clinton Anderson, a Democratic state assemblyman in Wisconsin, told the Times. "I want to make it a priority, but it's not the thing I heard on the doors I knocked."

Another question is what might happen in the courts if the compact actually kicks in. Notre Dame law professor Derek Muller has argued that the NPVIC would be unconstitutional without congressional approval — which, in his view, is required under the Constitution's Compact Clause.

"It's a very real possibility that enough states join this compact," Muller told the Times. But, he added, "there will be a lot of challenges."

articles.title: The model, the Grammy winner and the 'Dragon Ball Z' composer: Some of the midterms' big winners have fascinating backgrounds
articles.summary: Elections always introduce the American public to a sprawling cast of new political characters. This year's midterms were no different.
articles.body:
Every major election cycle serves as something of an introduction to a sprawling new cast of characters who have been elevated to national fame after winning one of the biggest races in the country. These midterms were no different.

Tuesday's election results featured a long list of new governors, senators, House members and other officials who many Americans likely learned about for the first time. The roster of breakout midterm winners includes some candidates with unexpected backgrounds, past jobs or family histories.

Here's a rundown on some of the more unique biographical nuggets from this year's group of newly elected lawmakers.

Iowa's next governor, Democrat Rob Sand, has a résumé that looks relatively by-the-book at first glance. He's currently serving as state auditor and previously worked in the Iowa attorney general's office. But go a bit further back, and you'll find some more unconventional elements in his bio. He worked as a model in the early 2000s, walking the runway for major fashion brands in Paris and Milan. He also coauthored a true crime book about "the largest lottery-rigging scheme in American history."

Nathan Johnson, a Democrat who was elected to become attorney general of Texas on Tuesday, has the legal and political credentials you'd typically expect from someone who's about to become a state's most important law enforcement official. But before he took part in this year's midterm blue wave, he spent his time thinking about Kamehameha Waves. Johnson is credited with composing the score for 67 episodes of the English dub of Dragon Ball Z , one of the most iconic anime series of all time.

Democrat Bobby Pulido was elected to represent Texas's 15th Congressional District, flipping a seat that had voted Republican for the first time ever two years ago back under Democratic control. Unlike some of the other candidates on this list, Pulido's unique background isn't hidden deep in the "personal life" section of his Wikipedia page.

He put his history as a Tejano music star front and center throughout his campaign. Since launching his music career in 1995, Pulido has released 15 albums and been awarded two Latin Grammys .

"For over 30 years, you played my music at your weddings, your quinceañeras, and your carne asadas," Pulido said in a message to Texas voters after being elected. "Tonight, you trusted me with something even bigger than a song, you trusted me with your future and I will work hard every day to honor it."

Another newly elected lawmaker whose old profession is anything but a secret is Mark Teixeira, a former Major League Baseball superstar who was elected to represent Texas's 21st District in the House.

Teixeira, a Republican, was named an All-Star three times during his 14-year career playing with the Texas Rangers and New York Yankees. Teixeira was a standout hitter and elite defender, earning five Gold Glove awards. He won a World Series title with the Yankees in 2009.

Before launching a career in politics that would make him Iowa's next senator, Democrat Josh Turek was one of the most successful wheelchair basketball players in history. Born with spina bifida, Turek began playing adaptive sports in his early teens and went on to become a standout star in college. He competed for Team USA at four Paralympic Games, winning two gold medals and a bronze. He was elected to the National Wheelchair Basketball Association Hall of Fame in 2023.

One of the biggest breakout names of the midterms was Keisha Lance Bottoms , a Georgia Democrat who will soon become the country's first Black woman governor. Bottoms's father was something of a pioneer himself in the world of music. Major Lance was a successful R&B singer with several hit songs in the 1960s, including "Monkey Time" and "Um, Um, Um, Um, Um, Um."

Those songs, both written by Curtis Mayfield, include early characteristics of what would eventually become known as soul music. After his popularity waned in the United States, Lance found renewed success in the United Kingdom as a key figure in the "Northern Soul" craze.

New Hampshire Democrat Chris Pappas will become the first openly gay man to serve in the U.S. Senate when he's sworn in early next year. In 2011, seven years before he first ran for Congress, Pappas appeared as a contestant on the game show Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?

Ironically, Pappas got stumped by a pair of questions connected to politics, which forced him to burn through two of his lifelines. He ended up taking home $17,500.

Pappas is also the grandson of a man who claims to have invented the chicken finger , and is still a co-owner of the family restaurant where that purported innovation took place.

There's a well-worn history of professional wrestlers pivoting to politics, but it's possible that no one has ever fused the two pursuits in the way that the next mayor of Providence, R.I., has. David Morales, a 28-year-old Democrat, performs in a local independent wrestling league under the persona "The Commissioner" — a corrupt, power-hungry politician designed to embody everything voters hate about elected officials.

Morales has said he believes there's "a lot of overlap" between wrestling and politics, "including showmanship, theater, athleticism, drama and humor." He also worries, though, that candidates who try too hard to emulate wrestlers risk leading themselves into "extremist rhetoric."
